text:
Almost a decade after Qatar Airways unveiled Qsuite, passengers still rate it as the best business class in the world.

Qatar Airways took first place for Preferred Business Class in the 2026 AirlineRatings.com Flyers’ Choice Awards, ahead of Emirates in second place and Singapore Airlines in third. Unlike AirlineRatings.com’s editorial awards, the Flyers’ Choice results are based entirely on votes from passengers.

The unique Qsuite has staying power. Airline business class seats have changed dramatically since Qatar Airways first unveiled the product in 2017. Privacy doors are more common, direct aisle access is expected and several airlines have introduced suites with larger screens, more storage and improved technology.

Yet passengers still picked Qsuite.

The product is now approaching its tenth anniversary and Qatar Airways is building on its success with the new Qsuite Next Gen.

Why Qatar Airways’ Qsuite transformed business class travel

Qatar Airways unveiled the original Qsuite at ITB Berlin in March 2017. It was an unusually ambitious business class product for the time.

Its headline feature was the industry’s first double bed in business class, but the product’s unique “Quad” format made it flexible to accommodate a variety of passengers. Qatar Airways included movable privacy panels with the four-seat arrangement that allowed families, friends or colleagues to create a shared space.

The alternating forward- and rear-facing 1-2-1 configuration was designed around flexibility rather than simply giving every passenger the same enclosed seat.

The airline offers four ways of using Qsuite: Single Suite, Twin Suite, Double Suite and The Quad.

Solo travellers can close the door and create a private room. Couples in selected centre seats can lower the divider between them and rest in a double bed. Groups of four can open all partitions around the centre seats to dine, work or socialise together.

Many competitors have added privacy doors to business class, but none have replicated the Qsuite’s ability to connect four individual seats in one space.

The first Qsuite-equipped Boeing 777 was displayed at the Paris Air Show in June 2017 before entering passenger service between Doha and London Heathrow on 24 June.

Qatar Airways then progressively expanded the product across its long-haul fleet and network.

Why Qsuite remains one of the world’s best business class products

Airline business class competition has intensified considerably since 2017.

British Airways introduced its Club Suite, Delta expanded its Delta One Suites and several other global carriers have developed private business class cabin products.

Cathay Pacific’s Aria Suite is one of the newest competitors. It ranked in first place among its competitors in North East Asia.

AirlineRatings.com CEO Sharon Petersen specifically highlighted it when discussing the 2026 results. “I expected Cathay Pacific to feature more strongly in Business Class because its Aria Suite is a spectacular product,” she stated. “However, these are the Flyers’ Choice Awards, so the results reflect the experiences of the travelling public rather than an editorial assessment.”

Qatar Airways finished ahead of its newer rivals in the passenger vote in part because the original concept anticipated where business class was heading and delivered something refreshing. It’s had time to build a positive reputation since.

Privacy doors, direct aisle access and fully flat beds have become standard expectations at the top end of the market. Qsuite offered all three years ago, while adding the double-bed and Quad configurations that remain distinctive.

That flexibility has helped prevent a nine-year-old seat from feeling its age.

Which Qatar Airways aircraft have Qsuite?

Qatar Airways has spent the years since Qsuite’s introduction refining its business class while experimenting with a variety of cabin products.

As a result, Qsuite has never been fitted across the entire Qatar Airways fleet. Aircraft type alone does not always guarantee the product, particularly among the airline’s Airbus A350s and Boeing 777s where business class can vary between QSuite and other private suites.

Qatar Airways also chose a different solution for its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners.

When the 787-9 entered service in 2021, the airline introduced an Adient Ascent-based Business Class Suite rather than installing the original Qsuite.

The 30-seat cabin is arranged 1-2-1 and retains many of the features passengers expect from Qatar Airways business class, including direct aisle access and sliding privacy doors. The seat converts into a 79-inch fully flat bed and includes wireless device charging. Centre passengers can also lower the divider between adjoining suites.

It is an excellent business class product in its own right, but it does not match the Qsuite’s Quad arrangement.

The airline’s next step is more ambitious.

What is Qatar Airway’s Qsuite Next Gen?

Qatar Airways revealed Qsuite Next Gen at the Farnborough International Airshow in July 2024.

The new Quad Suite provides more space for four passengers travelling together, with movable 4K OLED entertainment screens that can be repositioned to open the space. The dividers are also higher, providing more privacy for passengers flying on separate suites.

Qatar Airways has also developed a Companion Suite beside the window allowing two passengers to create a shared private space while both retain access to the view.

The airline says Qsuite Next Gen will offer wider and longer lie-flat beds, improved double beds, lockable storage drawers and touchscreen passenger control units. Entertainment screens will have Bluetooth connectivity.

It is essentially an evolution of the idea introduced in 2017. It offers an individual business class passenger a private suite and allows several seats to become a shared space for those travelling together.

Why Qsuite Next Gen has been delayed

Passengers have been waiting considerably longer than Qatar Airways originally expected to put Qsuite Next Gen into service.

The product was developed for Qatar Airways’ new Boeing 777-9 fleet. Qatar Airways has one of the world’s largest 777X commitments with 124 aircraft on order. In 2024, it announced that its future 777-9 business class cabins would feature Qsuite Next Gen.

Repeated delays to Boeing’s 777X programme have pushed back the arrival of the new cabin as well.

Qatar Airways is not alone in this 777X predicament. Emirates also developed its “game changer” first class for the 777X in 2018, and installed it on a few 777-300ERs amid delays with the new widebody programme. By the time Emirates gets its 777X aircraft, the unique first class product will also be a decade old.

Why Qsuite remains a business class leader nearly a decade later

Longevity is difficult in premium aircraft cabins.

Airlines generally have to design seats years before passengers first experience them, with certification, manufacturing, and aircraft production adding to the timeline. Fleet retrofit programmes can then keep a product flying for another decade or longer.

The intense competition to provide a superior product comes with the risk that an expensive new cabin can quickly appear dated.

Qsuite has avoided this problem because its biggest innovations were not features that competitors could easily match with larger screens or newer technology. The Qsuite focused on how passengers use the physical space around their seats.

Privacy for one passenger, a double bed for two, and a shared room for four remain useful features regardless of how quickly onboard technology changes.

The 2026 Flyers’ Choice result suggests passengers still value that formula. And with Qsuite Next Gen waiting in the wings, Qatar Airways is betting that the concept still has plenty of life left in it.

It is the primary artery connecting imported renewable feedstocks, including used cooking oil (UCO), vegetable oils, and other biofuel inputs.
It also moves finished renewable fuels from refineries to blending terminals throughout Germany and neighboring markets.
The Rhine's historically low water levels have exposed how vulnerable inland renewable fuel supply chains can become when critical transportation infrastructure is constrained.
As Europe moves into its strongest period of annual compliance demand, market participants will be watching more than energy prices.
text:
For decades, the Rhine has quietly served as one of Europe's most important trade corridors. Stretching from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea, the river connects the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) refining hub with industrial centers across Germany, France, and Switzerland.

Every year, millions of tons of fuels, chemicals, agricultural products, and feedstocks move along its waters. Today, however, historically low water levels are transforming the Rhine from a logistical advantage into a supply chain bottleneck.

Cargo vessels are being forced to sail with reduced loads or none at all. Meanwhile, freight rates have surged as available transport capacity shrinks.

Water levels at Kaub, one of the Rhine's most critical shipping chokepoints, have fallen to record lows. This prompted emergency measures across Germany to help offset supply disruptions.

For Europe's biofuel market, the implications extend well beyond transportation delays. They are reshaping feedstock availability, production economics, and renewable fuel pricing just as compliance demand begins to accelerate.

A River at the Center of Europe's Renewable Fuel Supply Chain

The Rhine is much more than a shipping lane for finished fuels.

It is the primary artery connecting imported renewable feedstocks, including used cooking oil (UCO), vegetable oils, and other biofuel inputs. It connects inland biodiesel and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) production facilities. It also moves finished renewable fuels from refineries to blending terminals throughout Germany and neighboring markets.

When barge traffic slows, the entire supply chain begins to tighten:

Feedstocks arrive later than planned.

Production schedules become more difficult to maintain.

Finished fuels struggle to reach inland blending locations.

Transportation costs rise.

Market participants begin competing for a smaller pool of immediately available supply.

The latest Prima CarbonZero analysis suggests these dynamics are already unfolding.

Logistics Are Becoming a Pricing Driver

Ordinarily, renewable fuels tend to move broadly in line with diesel markets. But not in this case.

Despite a sharp decline in gasoil prices recently, European biodiesel and HVO premiums continued to strengthen. Rather than responding primarily to falling fossil fuel prices, the market is increasingly responding to physical constraints on the availability of renewable fuels.

One of the largest challenges appears to be the inability to efficiently move feedstocks to inland rapeseed methyl ester (RME) plants. Simultaneously, this is limiting HVO deliveries to Germany's inland blending system.

In other words, the market is not simply paying for renewable feedstocks; it is paying for reliable access to those feedstocks. As logistics become constrained, biofuel premiums can remain elevated even when underlying petroleum markets soften.

Why Timing Matters

All of these disruptions come at a particularly sensitive moment for European compliance markets.

Historically, blending activity tends to strengthen during the second half of the year as obligated parties work toward meeting annual greenhouse gas reduction requirements. This seasonal increase in demand typically supports renewable fuel consumption.

This year, however, the market faces an additional challenge. If logistics remain constrained while compliance demand accelerates, buyers could encounter tighter physical availability precisely when blending requirements become most urgent.

Market participants continue to question whether Germany, Europe's largest biofuel market, faces a significant second-half blending requirement. Reduced opportunities for double-counting have narrowed compliance options. Limited carry-over volumes from previous years have added to the uncertainty.

Even the perception of stronger compliance demand can support prices when supply chains are already under pressure.

HVO Continues to Outperform

Hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) has been one of the strongest-performing products during the recent market rally.

While feedstock costs have increased only modestly, HVO values have climbed more rapidly. This has improved production margins for refiners. Widening production spread suggests demand for finished renewable fuel currently exceeds demand for imported feedstock alone.

Rhine-related logistical constraints reflect that German HVO supply disruptions remain an important risk. And that risk is even greater as we head into the peak compliance period.

Feedstocks Tell a Different Story

Not every segment of the market is behaving the same way, though.

UCO continues to attract strong demand, particularly for higher-quality feedstocks used in European renewable diesel production. At the same time, global competition remains intense. US renewable diesel producers are continuing to source competitively priced Chinese UCO despite recent policy adjustments favoring European material.

Rapeseed oil has also demonstrated remarkable resilience. Soybean oil has weakened amid comfortable global supply expectations. Conversely, rapeseed oil continues to find support from several factors:

Uncertain European harvest prospects

Ongoing disruptions to Ukrainian agricultural exports

Stronger North American canola demand

Higher expected production costs in future growing seasons

These structural supply concerns help establish a firmer price floor for Europe's conventional biodiesel market.

Weather Now Becoming a Market Variable

The Rhine's current challenges illustrate a broader trend affecting commodity markets worldwide. Extreme weather events are increasingly influencing not only agricultural production but also transportation infrastructure.

Low river levels can reduce effective freight capacity long before waterways become completely unnavigable. Barges often remain operational but with significantly reduced cargo loads. Consequently, this increases transportation costs throughout the supply chain.

Recent reports indicate freight rates on the Rhine have climbed sharply. Accordingly, governments and industries are implementing emergency contingency measures to maintain industrial supply chains.

Renewable fuel margins often depend on the efficient movement of relatively low-value bulk feedstocks. Consequently, these logistical disruptions can quickly become significant pricing events.

Looking Ahead

The biofuel market's recent resilience highlights an important shift in market dynamics. Rather than being driven solely by crude oil or diesel prices, renewable fuels are increasingly responding to a combination of compliance obligations, feedstock availability, logistics, and weather-related disruptions.

The Rhine's historically low water levels have exposed how vulnerable inland renewable fuel supply chains can become when critical transportation infrastructure is constrained. As Europe moves into its strongest period of annual compliance demand, market participants will be watching more than energy prices.

They'll also be watching river gauges.

This year, one of the most important indicators for Europe's biofuel market may not be found on an energy exchange but on the Rhine itself.

Stay Ahead of the Biofuels Market in Q4 2026

The biofuels market moves incredibly fast with multiple factors impacting it. From climate events to geopolitical strife, keeping up with the signals can quickly become an immense challenge.

Fortunately, ResourceWise can help.

Join us on September 3 for our Biofuels Market Outlook: Q4 2026 webinar, where Mat Stone will break down the forces shaping the market as we head into the final quarter of the year. The session will examine what changed during Q3, where pricing and market fundamentals may be heading next, and the opportunities and risks emerging across key biofuels and feedstock markets.

The webinar will cover developments across the US, Europe, and Asia, including 45Z and evolving US guidance, RED III, US-Europe trade dynamics, and Chinese HVO exports. We'll also assess tightening and oversupplied feedstock markets, emerging advanced feedstocks, and the latest developments in sustainable aviation fuel and marine biofuels.

Register for the webinar to gain the market context and forward-looking insight you need to prepare for Q4 2026.

DUBLIN AIRPORT

The Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Act 2026 (PDF, 580 KB) has been signed into law by President Connolly. It empowers the Minister for Transport to make an order to address the 32 million passenger cap at Dublin Airport.

REFUEL EU

European Union (REFUELEU Aviation) (Enforcement) Regulations 2026 (PDF, 222 KB) implement enforcement of the EU ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation (EU 2023/2405) in Ireland. The Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) and the National Oil Reserves Agency (NORA) are the competent authorities, with NORA enforcing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply obligations and the IAA enforcing aircraft operator and airport managing body obligations. Provisions include the following:

Aviation fuel suppliers failing to meet minimum SAF or synthetic fuel shares face a fine of two to four times the price differential between conventional and SAF fuel, multiplied by the non-compliant fuel quantity.

Aircraft operators failing to uplift required fuel quantities face a fine of two to four times the average fuel price multiplied by the yearly non-tanked quantity, with a right to seek an exemption.

Airport managing bodies failing to ensure adequate SAF access face fines of up to €100,000 (airports under three million passengers/year) or €250,000 (three million or more).

Parties may make representations within 21 days of a notification and appeal a confirmed decision to the appropriate court within 14 days.

RENEWABLE ENERGY DIRECTIVE (TRANSPORT FUEL)

European Union (Transport) (Renewable Energy) Regulations 2026 (PDF, 153 KB) transpose further elements of the Renewable Energy Directive (at Articles 25-27, 30 and 31a) into Irish law by updating definitions and cross-references across the biofuel/renewable transport fuel obligation regime, introducing the new RFNBO obligation category, tightening sustainability-certification evidentiary requirements, and revoking a now-superseded 2017 greenhouse gas reporting instrument.

CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE ACT

The Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 is commenced, as we outline in our Insights Blog post: Critical Infrastructure Act 2026 commenced. Projects designated as critical infrastructure projects include MetroLink, the Cork Area Commuter Rail Programme, and the Galway City Ring Road project.

SKOKIE, Ill., Aug. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- LanzaTech Global, Inc. (NASDAQ: LNZA) (“LanzaTech” or the “Company”), a carbon management solutions company, today reported its financial and operating results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026.

Second Quarter 2026 Financial and Operational Highlights (comparisons vs. Second Quarter 2025)

Revenue of $9.0 million, down 1% compared to $9.1 million

Operating Expenses of $11.7 million, improved by 67% compared to $35.1 million

Net Income of $184.3 million, compared to a net loss of $32.5 million, primarily reflecting a significant non-cash unrealized gain on the Company's investment in SGLT.

Adjusted EBITDA of $(7.6) million improved by approximately 74% compared to $(29.7) million

Management Comments:

Dr. Jennifer Holmgren, CEO of LanzaTech, stated “Our Second Quarter results reflect the actions we have taken to reshape LanzaTech for the current market. We have reduced costs, renegotiated key contracts and refocused capital spend as we move from an R&D-led model toward commercial project deployment. These actions are improving our year over year operating results and creating a more disciplined platform for revenue growth and long-term profitability.”

Dr. Holmgren continued, “As we execute our near-term cost reduction and profitability improvement strategy, we continue to advance milestones that support commercialization and future value capture. Our work towards the world’s first ISCC EU certification for recycled carbon fuel is a critical step in opening mandated European fuel markets to CarbonSmart ethanol. We believe this creates new commercial optionality across multiple end markets. SAF remains a core medium-term opportunity, supported by leading alcohol-to-jet technology, while certified carbon-smart ethanol gives us near-term access to direct-use markets such as marine and road transport. That breadth is a strategic asset, giving us flexibility, resilience, and multiple paths to monetize our technology today, while certification work like ISCC EU keeps us well positioned in mandated markets as they expand. Together, these markets support our focus on converting commercial progress into revenue growth and a clearer path to sustainable profitability.”

Key Strategic and Operational Updates:

Selected North Sea Port, Ghent for FLITE SAF facility: In May, LanzaTech selected North Sea Port, Ghent, Belgium as the permanent site for Europe’s first commercial-scale Alcohol-to-Jet sustainable aviation fuel facility using the LanzaJet ATJ process, targeting 79,000 tonnes of SAF and 9,000 tonnes of renewable diesel annually and marking a major de-risking milestone toward FID with the planned Environmental Impact Assessment scoping notification.

LanzaTech estimates that the FLITE project carries the potential to deliver approximately $115 million in annualized offtaking revenues, with significant additional revenue opportunity streams.

LanzaTech is currently undergoing the world's first ISCC EU certification pathway for recycled carbon fuels in China, working with ISCC and other stakeholders to establish the methodology, carbon accounting, and traceability standards for this emerging fuel category. ISCC EU certification verifies compliance with the EU's Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) and is also recognized by the UK's Department for Transport, making it a gateway to both mandated markets. This work is foundational to market access for recycled carbon fuel projects and future certifications as the category scales.

Added to the Russell 3000 Index: LanzaTech was added to the Russell 3000 Index, effective June 29, 2026, also placing the Company in the Russell 2000 small-cap index and expanding visibility with institutional investors and passive index funds.

Successful IPO and post-listing value creation of SGLT joint venture: In June, Beijing Shougang LanzaTech Technology Co., Ltd. completed its IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, raising approximately US$75 million in gross proceeds for SGLT and implying a market capitalization of approximately US$750 million upon listing. The Company did not sell any shares in the offering and did not receive any proceeds. Following completion of the offering, the Company held, through its subsidiary, 33,520,231 H Shares of Shougang LanzaTech, representing approximately 8.38% of the JV’s total issued share capital upon listing. Driven by strong initial trading volume, the JV's market capitalization escalated to roughly US$1.32 billion as of August 12, at which point LanzaTech's retained equity held an estimated market value of around US$110 million. This provides public-market validation that LanzaTech-originated platforms can scale in commercially demanding sectors, while also demonstrating the potential value of LanzaTech’s strategy of combining technology licensing with equity participation in commercial projects.

Launched BRIGHT partnership to accelerate carbon-to-value biotechnology: LanzaTech entered a multi-year collaboration with BRIGHT at the Technical University of Denmark to design and install a next-generation C1 biofoundry, supporting development of technologies that convert CO2, CO and methane into fuels, chemicals and materials.

Net income was $169.6 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, primarily due to a $208.1 million non-cash unrealized gain on the Company's investment in SGLT, compared to net loss of $51.7 million for the six months ended June 30, 2025. Adjusted EBITDA (1) loss decreased to $15.5 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, compared to Adjusted EBITDA loss of $60.2 million for the six months ended June 30, 2025, reflecting meaningful progress in underlying operating performance, driven by disciplined cost optimization initiatives.

Revenue

Reported total revenue of $9.0 million for the second quarter of 2026, compared to total revenue of $9.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. The decrease was primarily attributable to a $1.0 million decrease in revenue from Joint Development Agreements (“JDA”) and a $0.5 million reduction in revenue received from LanzaJet for their sublicensing of our technology, partially offset by a $1.4 million increase in engineering and other services revenue.

Engineering and other services revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $3.3 million, compared to $1.9 million in the second quarter of 2025, reflecting the initiation of new customer projects and increased engineering activity.

JDA revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $0.3 million, compared to $1.3 million in the second quarter of 2025, due to the completion of projects with existing customers.

Licensing revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $0.6 million, compared to $1.1 million in the second quarter of 2025, due to the decrease in licensing revenue received from LanzaJet for their sublicensing of our technology.

Contract research revenue in the second quarter of 2026 was $1.0 million, consistent with the second quarter of 2025.

CarbonSmart revenue was $3.8 million in the second quarter of 2026, consistent with the second quarter of 2025.

Cost of Revenue

Cost of revenue was $7.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $6.2 million in the second quarter of 2025. The increase reflects a greater proportion of engineering services and product-related activity in the current period, particularly CarbonSmart product sales and customer project execution, resulting in a different revenue and cost mix than the prior-year period.

Operating Expense

For the second quarter of 2026 operating expense was $11.7 million, as compared to $35.1 million for the same period in the prior year. The decrease was primarily due to a decrease in personnel and contractor expenses related to R&D projects and administrative operations, reflecting headcount reductions implemented during 2025 as part of the Company’s broader cost optimization initiatives. These reductions are designed to align the Company’s cost base with its commercialization priorities and support its path to profitability.

Net income (loss)

Net income for the second quarter of 2026 was $184.3 million, compared with a net loss of $32.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily driven by a $208.1 million non-cash unrealized gain recognized on the Company's investment in SGLT resulting from the remeasurement of the investment to fair value following the investee’s public listing and subsequent changes in the quoted market price during the quarter. The quarter also benefited from the impact of the Company's transformation, cost optimization and organizational streamlining initiatives, which reduced operating expenses and contributed to a significant improvement in Adjusted EBITDA compared with the prior-year period.

Adjusted EBITDA

Adjusted EBITDA loss was $7.6 million as compared to adjusted EBITDA loss of $29.7 million in the second quarter of 2025. The improvement was primarily attributable to the benefits of the Company's transformation, cost optimization and organizational streamlining initiatives implemented during 2025, which resulted in significantly lower personnel, contractor, legal and other operating expenses.

Balance Sheet and Liquidity

As of June 30, 2026, the Company had $48.9 million in total cash and restricted cash compared to total cash, restricted cash, and investments of $17.1 million as of December 31, 2025. The increase reflects our issuance of common stock for gross proceeds of $50.0 million in the six months ended June 30, 2026, partially offset by continued use of cash to fund operating activities and our $3.0 million purchase of LanzaJet Series A Preferred Stock.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures

text:
SAF project targets fourth-quarter investment decision

→ Nebius' Q2 Beat Shows the AI Bottleneck Is Capacity, Not Demand

The company continues to advance its sustainable aviation fuel project toward a final investment decision in the fourth quarter. On June 19, Tidewater executed a new initiative agreement with the Government of British Columbia that is intended to provide additional BC-LCFS credits for critical pre-final-investment-decision work.

The work includes engineering, regulatory advancement, preservation of vendor and fabrication capacity, and maintaining the project schedule, Baines said. Tidewater expects to receive the BC-LCFS credits in the third and fourth quarters as milestones are achieved.

In response to an analyst question, Baines said a final investment decision depends on a supportive regulatory environment, including targeted amendments under the Clean Fuel Regulations and other potential programs supporting Canada's sustainable aviation fuel sector. He put the project's estimated capital cost at about C$1.2 billion and said the company has completed a class 3 front-end engineering design study.

Baines said the project would have a three-year construction period and could enter service in 2030. Tidewater expects it could contribute funds from operating cash flow during construction and is also evaluating potential investment from a First Nations partner and other interested parties.

Guidance rises as leverage declines

Tidewater increased its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance for the renewables business to C$130 million to C$140 million. The company raised consolidated adjusted EBITDA guidance to C$230 million to C$250 million, up 20% at the midpoint from its prior outlook.

Quartly attributed the higher guidance to increased facility utilization, sustained strength in forward crack spreads, and improved renewable diesel and emissions-credit pricing. Forecast 2026 capital expenditures for Tidewater Renewables remain unchanged at C$2 million to C$3 million.

The company reduced Tidewater Renewables' debt by C$13.5 million during the second quarter. Its debt-to-adjusted-EBITDA ratio was 1.47 times as of June 30, while the consolidated company's ratio was 1.7 times, within its target range of 1.2 times to 2.5 times.

Quartly said the company intends to direct free cash flow primarily toward debt reduction while maintaining its disciplined capital program.

Broader Tidewater operations benefit from strong refining markets

Tidewater Midstream generated deconsolidated adjusted EBITDA of C$32.9 million in the second quarter, up C$7.3 million from the first quarter. The improvement was driven mainly by higher crack spreads at the Prince George Refinery, partly offset by realized losses on crack-spread hedges.

Prince George Refinery throughput averaged 10,032 barrels per day because of a planned 17-day partial outage in April. Excluding that outage, throughput averaged 12,060 barrels per day, or 101% of design capacity. The Prince George crack spread averaged C$118 per barrel, 16% higher than in the first quarter.

Tidewater has hedged about half of its crack-spread exposure from April through December 2026. It also added hedges during the second half of July covering approximately 40% of its 2027 crack-spread exposure at fixed prices that Baines said were significantly above mid-cycle pricing and 2026 realized hedge pricing.

Baines said Tidewater will continue pursuing non-core asset sales, prioritizing assets that do not fit its strategy or generate appropriate returns, while focusing on refinery and HDRD utilization, midstream volumes, commercial offtakes and the advancement of the sustainable aviation fuel project.

text:
Brazil has issued regulations for its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandate, setting the framework for airlines to begin reducing greenhouse gas emissions from domestic flights from 2027.

The decree, published by the Brazilian government on August 12, establishes rules for the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program, known as ProBioQAV. The programme was created under Brazil’s Fuel of the Future Law, enacted in October 2024, Ethanol Producer Magazine reported.

Under ProBioQAV, domestic airline operators will be required to achieve a 1% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in 2027, with the target increasing progressively to 10% by 2037.

The programme also allows a book-and-claim system for tracking SAF’s environmental attributes. Under this model, the physical fuel and its associated environmental benefits can be traded separately among different commercial operators and buyers.

The new regulations allow the carbon intensity of SAF to be calculated using either Brazil’s REnovaBio carbon-intensity calculation tool or the International Civil Aviation Organization’s CORISA methodology.

Brazil’s National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) and the National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC) have been directed to issue additional regulations needed to implement the SAF mandate by December 18, 2026.

Potential ethanol demand

The mandate could create a significant new market for ethanol-based SAF. Data previously published by UNICA, Brazil’s sugarcane industry association, estimates that ProBioQAV could generate demand for about 1.2 billion litres of alcohol-based SAF.

Meeting the programme’s emissions-reduction targets could require around 2 billion litres of ethanol as a feedstock for SAF production, according to UNICA estimates.

The new framework is expected to provide greater clarity to airlines, fuel producers and other participants preparing for Brazil’s SAF market, with the detailed implementation rules to be issued later this year.

title: Australia's air traffic future - UNSW Sydney
description:
Air traffic control is about capability, not just numbers It is tempting to think of an air traffic controller shortage like any other workforce shortage: recruit more people and fill the vacancies.
Selection and recruitment of new air traffic controllers is only the beginning.
Safety involves the whole system We tend to talk about aviation through its most visible actors: pilots and air traffic controllers.
A local disruption can become a global problem Air traffic management is also globally connected.
This is why resilient air traffic management matters beyond one airport or one country.
text:
Air traffic control is about capability, not just numbers

It is tempting to think of an air traffic controller shortage like any other workforce shortage: recruit more people and fill the vacancies.

It is not that simple.

Controllers perform a central role in one of the world’s most safety-critical and interconnected industries. Selection and recruitment of new air traffic controllers is only the beginning.

We need to attract motivated candidates who see themselves as well suited to the profession, select those with the right aptitude, train and qualify them effectively, and continue supporting their operational and professional development throughout their careers.

I think of this as a capability lifecycle.

Qualification should never be considered the end of learning. Controllers need to continue developing as traffic, procedures and technologies change.

They also need to remain prepared for situations that, fortunately, may rarely occur in real life: emergencies, severe weather, communication failures, equipment problems and unexpected combinations of events.

We cannot wait for a real emergency to provide that experience.

This is why high-fidelity real-time simulation is so valuable. It is not only a place to teach basic skills with teamwork competencies, but can expose experienced professionals to unusual and demanding situations and allow them to practise responding under pressure without creating risk in the real aviation system.

After many years working with ATC simulation, I see this as one of its greatest strengths: we can practise the situations we hope never happen.

Australia and new aviation technology

Australia is investing in new aviation infrastructure, digital aerodrome services and increasingly automated air traffic management systems, including developments associated with Western Sydney International Airport.

These investments create major opportunities for safety, efficiency and capacity. But every technology transition also has a human side.

Engineers often talk about Technology Readiness Levels. We should also think seriously about Human Readiness Levels — whether the people who will operate, supervise and work alongside new technology are ready for it.

Technology readiness and human readiness need to progress together.

There is little value in highly mature technology if operational staff have not had enough opportunity to understand it, recognise its limitations and practise what to do when it behaves unexpectedly.

This becomes even more important as artificial intelligence and decision-support systems enter aviation. Real time, human in the loop ATC simulation can add value safely in developing and validating new AI tools and decision aids for controllers. For instance, digital tower simulator can be deployed as a digital twin of the new aerodrome concepts to validate and improve new ideas and procedures.

The future is therefore not simply humans versus automation.

It is increasingly humans working with automation.

Safety involves the whole system

We tend to talk about aviation through its most visible actors: pilots and air traffic controllers.

But safe aviation involves many more people.

Airport operators, engineers, ground handlers, tug drivers, airlines, safety specialists, regulators, technology providers and researchers all contribute.

Safe aviation is not created by controllers and pilots alone. It is created by people and organisations working effectively together.

This is why simulation should increasingly go beyond training individuals in isolation.

We can put controllers, pilots, airport personnel and other operators into the same simulated emergency and examine where communication works, where it fails, how workload changes and whether everyone develops the same understanding of the situation.

We can also learn from events that have already occurred.

Using investigation findings and operational records, incidents and accidents can be reconstructed in simulated environments. We may never reproduce every detail perfectly, but we can recreate known or plausible conditions and examine how communication, workload, procedures, technology and decision-making interacted.

Then we can test alternatives.

What happens if a procedure changes? What if information is displayed differently? What if another safety barrier is introduced?

That turns an occurrence into an opportunity for systematic learning.

Simulation can therefore be much more than a training device. It can be a training environment, research laboratory, safety-learning platform and testbed for future aviation systems.

A local disruption can become a global problem

Air traffic management is also globally connected.

A delay in Sydney does not necessarily end when the aircraft leaves Sydney.

The aircraft may arrive late at its next destination. That can affect another flight, crew duty times, passenger connections, gates and airport resources, and have a snowball effect for all stakeholders.

One disruption can propagate through the network.

This is why resilient air traffic management matters beyond one airport or one country. A local operational constraint can have national and international consequences.

Australia should bring its capabilities together

At UNSW Canberra, we have established an air traffic control simulation capability that allows complex airport and airspace operations to be reproduced without introducing risk into live operations.

But the opportunity is larger than one university or one simulator.

Australia already has considerable capability spread across Airservices, airports, airlines, Defence, regulators, government, universities, research organisations and technology companies.

We should connect those capabilities more deliberately.

text:
CoverCress Inc., developer of the winter oilseed crop CoverCress®, revealed that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has approved renewable fuel pathways for its product under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) programme.

Under the Chevron Geismar CoverCress Pathways, EPA has determined that renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced from CoverCress® oil qualify for biomass-based diesel (D4) Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs).

Renewable naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) produced through the same pathways qualify for advanced biofuel (D5) RINs.

RINs are the tradable credits obligated parties use to meet RFS obligations, so pathway approval is what allows fuel made from CoverCress oil to be sold into the RFS market and earn credit value.

The approval arrives as CoverCress prepares for its first commercial crush in early 2027, giving growers, grain handlers, processors and fuel producers regulatory certainty as they plan for the crop’s expanding role in the renewable fuel supply chain.

“The recognition of CoverCress® oil as an approved feedstock pathway under the Renewable Fuel Standard strengthens the commercial foundation for adoption across the value chain — from growers to grain handlers, processors and fuel producers,” said CoverCress CEO Jim Hedges. “This is a major milestone for our company and stakeholders. We appreciate the thorough review conducted by EPA and the commitment of industry partners who have helped advance the development of this innovative crop.”

As a winter annual oilseed, CoverCress® is planted after traditional cash crops and harvested before spring planting, giving growers an additional source of farm income while providing soil cover during otherwise fallow periods.

The crop is being developed to supply fuel producers with a new, scalable and domestic source of renewable fuel feedstock.

Headlines

EU approves $335 million to expand sustainable aviation fuel production in the Netherlands. The European Commission has approved around $335 million in Dutch State aid to support the development and production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The funding will focus on advanced bio-SAF and synthetic e-SAF, with supported projects expected to produce around 285 kilotonnes of SAF annually. The schemes will run from 2027 to 2031, supporting Europe’s efforts to increase cleaner fuel supply as aviation decarbonisation requirements tighten. How is this business relevant? Public funding could help SAF projects overcome high upfront costs and bring less mature technologies closer to commercial scale. For airlines, fuel producers and investors, expanding production capacity will be increasingly important as EU mandates drive demand for lower-carbon aviation fuels, creating new investment opportunities across the SAF value chain.

India drives global rise in planned coal production despite slowing demand. Global plans for new coal mines rose sharply in 2025, with proposed projects capable of adding 2.5 billion tonnes of annual production (11% more than the previous year). The increase was driven largely by India, particularly Odisha and Jharkhand, as the country looks to expand coal supply to meet rising electricity demand. The trend contrasts with the wider market: new mine openings are falling, global coal demand is expected to slow, and wind and solar have now overtaken coal in global electricity generation. How is this business relevant? The growing gap between planned coal capacity and slowing long-term demand raises the risk of stranded assets and weaker returns for new mining projects. For energy companies, lenders and investors, decisions on coal expansion will increasingly need to account for the falling cost of renewables, changing electricity markets and the possibility that future demand may not justify today’s investment pipeline.

$182 Million fund targets green hydrogen growth in Southern Africa. Climate Fund Managers has raised $182 million at the first close of its SA-H2 Fund, aimed at accelerating green hydrogen and industrial decarbonisation projects across Southern Africa. The fund brings together public and private capital to support green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol projects, as well as efforts to reduce emissions in sectors such as steel, fertilisers, chemicals and e-fuels. How is this business relevant? The fund could help overcome one of the biggest barriers to green hydrogen development: financing early-stage projects. By reducing investment risk, the blended finance model could attract more institutional capital into clean infrastructure and help Southern Africa turn its strong renewable energy potential into new industrial and export opportunities.

Google opens new funding for carbon removal and methane research. Google has opened applications for its 2026 Climate R&D Awards, offering up to $500,000 per project to advance carbon removal and reduce other powerful greenhouse gases such as methane. Funding will support research across areas including ocean carbon removal, biochar, carbon capture, methane reduction, blue carbon and climate-focused agriculture. Applications are open until 25 September 2026, with funding expected by the end of the year. How is this business relevant? The programme could help emerging climate technologies move from research towards commercial use by addressing challenges such as cost, scalability and reliable measurement. For businesses and investors, it also highlights where innovation and funding are increasingly being directed as demand grows for credible carbon removal and emissions reduction solutions.

Malaysia targets $21.5 billion in energy savings as power demand grows. Malaysia has extended its national energy efficiency strategy to 2035, targeting around $21.5 billion in savings and an 11.6% reduction in energy demand compared with business-as-usual projections. The plan is expected to avoid 26.1 million tonnes of CO₂e emissions and comes as rapid growth in AI, data centres and other energy-intensive industries puts increasing pressure on the country’s electricity system. How is this business relevant? Rising power demand makes energy efficiency increasingly important for both cost management and business growth. The plan could create new opportunities in efficient cooling, energy management, building technologies and industrial equipment, while encouraging large energy users to invest in solutions that lower electricity costs and reduce pressure on the grid.

EU packaging rules bring new PFAS restrictions and tougher waste targets. New EU packaging rules have started to apply, including strict limits on PFAS in food-contact packaging such as takeaway containers, food wrappers and pizza boxes. The wider regulation will also introduce new requirements for recyclability, reuse, labelling and single-use packaging, as the EU targets a 5% reduction in packaging waste by 2030 and 15% by 2040, compared with 2018 levels. How is this business relevant? Companies selling packaged products in the EU will need to rethink materials, packaging design and supply chains as the new requirements are phased in. While this means additional compliance and investment, it could also create opportunities for recyclable packaging, reuse systems and alternative materials, as demand for more circular solutions grows across Europe.

Norway moves to speed up wind and grid expansion as power demand rises. Norway plans to halve the time needed to develop electricity grids and accelerate approvals for new onshore wind projects as demand for clean power grows. Renewable capacity expansion has slowed significantly in recent years, while industrial electrification and new data centres are putting increasing pressure on the country’s electricity system. The government hopes simpler permitting and stronger incentives for local communities will help unlock new projects. How is this business relevant? Access to sufficient electricity and grid capacity is becoming increasingly important for companies planning new facilities or electrifying existing operations. Faster development could unlock investment in renewable energy, grids and low-carbon industry, although local acceptance and grid constraints will remain important factors for developers and investors.

Germany seeks constitutional change to strengthen climate adaptation funding. Germany’s Environment Minister Carsten Schneider wants to amend the country’s constitution to make climate adaptation a shared responsibility across federal, state and local governments. The change would allow the federal government to directly fund measures such as cooling systems, urban shade and other heat protection infrastructure. The proposal follows a summer of record-breaking heatwaves that have affected public health, disrupted river transport and put pressure on supply chains. How is this business relevant? The proposal signals that climate adaptation is becoming an economic and infrastructure priority, not only an environmental issue. Greater federal funding could accelerate investment in resilient buildings, cooling and urban infrastructure, while helping businesses and cities prepare for growing disruption from extreme heat, water shortages and other physical climate risks.

Graph of the week: Japan’s shift from voluntary to mandatory climate disclosure

Japan’s transition to mandatory sustainability disclosure shows how climate reporting is moving from largely qualitative commitments towards more rigorous, auditable emissions data. From 2027, the largest companies on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market will begin reporting under SSBJ standards, including Scope 3 emissions across all 15 GHG Protocol categories.

The challenge extends well beyond reporting deadlines. Scope 3 typically represents around 75% of corporate emissions, while 66.1% of companies still use spreadsheets in some form to measure it, highlighting the gap between increasingly demanding disclosure requirements and existing data infrastructure.

Japan’s experience illustrates a broader shift: mandatory disclosure increasingly requires companies to build reliable emissions data and supplier-level visibility into their core operations rather than treating sustainability reporting as a standalone annual exercise.

Deep dive: ensuring equitable transitions and protecting vulnerable communities in the workforce

The transition to a low-carbon and digitally enabled economy is reshaping labour markets, business models and regional economies. While it can generate substantial employment and investment opportunities, the benefits and costs are unlikely to be distributed evenly. Workers in carbon-intensive sectors, low-income households, informal employment, rural areas and regions dependent on a small number of industries may face disproportionate risks from restructuring, automation, rising living costs and skills displacement. A credible transition therefore needs to address not only emissions reduction, but also employment security, income protection, access to skills, worker voice and the resilience of affected communities.

The scale of the employment opportunity is significant. At least 16.6 million people were directly or indirectly employed in renewable energy globally in 2024, the highest level recorded to date. However, job creation in expanding sectors does not automatically benefit workers losing employment in declining industries. The quality, location, accessibility and pay of new jobs are critical, particularly where workers cannot easily relocate or afford lengthy periods of retraining.

Who is most exposed?

Vulnerability is shaped by more than an individual’s occupation. Workers may face heightened exposure where they have limited formal qualifications, insecure employment, low savings, restricted access to transport or digital technology, caring responsibilities, disabilities or discrimination based on gender, race, age or migration status. Communities can also be vulnerable when local tax revenues, public services and supply chains depend heavily on fossil fuels, heavy industry, mining, agriculture or other transition-sensitive activities.

Climate impacts themselves are already affecting the world of work. Heat stress, extreme weather, reduced productivity and damage to infrastructure can undermine livelihoods before formal industrial restructuring takes place. The burden is often greatest for lower-income workers, who tend to have fewer opportunities to move, retrain or absorb temporary income losses. This creates a dual responsibility for employers and policymakers: protect people from the physical effects of climate change while ensuring that decarbonisation policies do not deepen existing inequalities.

The transition also has a strong gender and inclusion dimension. Women, migrants and minority groups are frequently over-represented in lower-paid, temporary or less secure roles, while remaining under-represented in many technical and energy occupations. The risk is that new green and digital jobs reproduce existing labour-market segregation unless recruitment, training, pay and promotion systems are deliberately designed to widen access. A case study from Brazil illustrates how targeted community training and hiring programmes can support women’s entry into traditionally male-dominated electricity roles, although such initiatives need to be scaled beyond individual companies.

From retraining to transition security

Re-skilling is important, but it is not a complete just-transition strategy. Training is unlikely to be effective if workers cannot afford time away from paid employment, if courses are poorly matched to local vacancies, or if employers continue to require experience that displaced workers do not yet possess. Effective programmes should therefore link skills provision to credible job pathways, recognised qualifications, apprenticeships, paid learning time and commitments from employers to recruit from affected communities.

Businesses should begin with a workforce and place-based impact assessment. This means mapping which roles, facilities, suppliers and communities may be affected by decarbonisation, automation or business-model changes. The assessment should identify groups likely to experience the greatest harm, including contractors and agency workers, rather than focusing solely on permanent employees. It should then inform measures such as redeployment, early access to training, income support, enhanced redundancy arrangements, relocation assistance, flexible work and partnerships with local colleges or employment services.

Worker participation is equally important. Consultation should take place before major decisions are finalised, not after closures, redundancies or technology deployments have been announced. Collective bargaining, works councils, trade unions, community organisations and representative groups can provide information that management teams may miss, especially concerning informal work, subcontracting and barriers faced by marginalised workers. The European Parliament’s proposed framework for a just transition in the world of work highlights training during working hours, worker consultation, collective bargaining, health and safety and protection against unfair dismissal as important elements of a fair transition.

Corporate responsibility and reporting

For companies, workforce equity should be integrated into transition planning rather than treated as a separate corporate social responsibility initiative. A credible plan should explain how emissions reduction measures affect employment, skills, wages, health and safety, worker representation and local communities. It should also state who is accountable, how resources are allocated and how progress will be monitored.

The European Sustainability Reporting Standards provide a relevant reporting framework. ESRS S1, which covers the undertaking’s own workforce, addresses working conditions, secure employment, working time, adequate wages, social dialogue, collective bargaining, health and safety, equal treatment, training and skills. It also recognises that climate transition plans can create negative impacts such as restructuring and employment loss, as well as positive opportunities through job creation and re-skilling.

Companies should not rely on aggregate headcount or average training expenditure to demonstrate fairness. More decision-useful indicators include the percentage of affected workers redeployed, training completion and placement rates, pay and benefit changes after redeployment, job-quality measures, turnover among vulnerable groups, collective-bargaining coverage, injury rates, grievance-resolution outcomes and the share of new transition-related jobs filled by local residents. Data should be disaggregated where legally and operationally appropriate by gender, age, disability, employment status, geography and other relevant characteristics.

Human-rights due diligence is also relevant across supply chains. A company may reduce direct operational emissions while shifting social costs to contractors, suppliers, miners, logistics workers or communities dependent on its purchasing decisions. Due diligence should therefore examine the effects of sourcing changes, supplier consolidation, technology adoption and procurement price pressure. It should include meaningful consultation, accessible grievance channels and remediation where adverse impacts occur. The UN Global Compact emphasises that companies should prioritise risks to people and planet, conduct ongoing due diligence and provide effective channels for concerns and remedy.

Abstract

Maritime decarbonization is increasingly urgent as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) extends carbon pricing to liner shipping. This study develops an AI-assisted bilevel framework combining Bayesian Optimization (BO) and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to link an emission-indexed support path, a unit-consistent Marginal Abatement Cost–Total Number of Allowances in Circulation–Market Stability Reserve (MAC–TNAC–MSR) feedback mechanism, and discrete carrier network responses. In the Asia–Europe case, a representative best-evaluated policy reduces cumulative physical and ETS-covered emissions by 28.39% and 32.94%, respectively, relative to a matched nine-hub baseline, while increasing resource cost by only 0.213%. It captures 85.91% of the same-constraint short-run abatement potential. In an exact 248-policy micro-instance, BO achieves a 0.00% median optimality gap, a 4.35% mean gap, and an 80.0% exact-hit rate across 30 seeds under a common 20-evaluation budget. These results demonstrate the sample efficiency of BO–MILP for discontinuous maritime policy-response problems and provide practical guidance for designing support policies that promote lower-emission vessel deployment without substantial additional resource costs.

1 Introduction

Maritime transport carries more than 80% of world merchandise trade by volume and accounts for approximately 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it indispensable to international trade but difficult to decarbonize ( IMO, 2025). Ships monitored under the EU Monitoring, Reporting and Verification system emitted 135.5 Mt CO2 in 2022 ( European Commission, 2024). Since January 2024, maritime transport has been progressively incorporated into the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), with allowance-surrender obligations increasing from 40% of verified emissions in 2024 to 100% from 2026 onward ( European Commission, 2025a). Early implementation monitoring covers approximately 12,000 large ships and has also examined potential avoidance behavior ( European Commission, 2025b). More broadly, evidence from carbon-pricing programs shows that their effectiveness depends on policy credibility, available abatement channels, and complementary instruments ( Döbbeling-Hildebrandt et al., 2024). Carbon regulation has therefore become an important determinant of shipping costs and operational decisions.

Recent methodological developments provide useful foundations for analyzing this transition. Data-driven studies have applied ensemble learning and machine-learning methods to ship energy-consumption prediction, emissions forecasting, and clean-energy shipbuilding ( Xu et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025c; Xu et al., 2026). Research on ESG-constrained digital technology adoption further emphasizes the importance of coordination among shipping stakeholders ( Qi et al., 2026), while graph-based assignment models demonstrate the value of preserving network topology and flow-conservation relationships ( Xiao G. et al., 2026). Bilevel optimization offers a complementary approach for representing sequential decisions between policy designers and transport operators ( Qi et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2023). Such models are particularly relevant to shipping, where regulatory signals interact with long-lived assets, discrete operational decisions, and sector-wide decarbonization pathways ( Müller-Casseres et al., 2024).

The maritime literature has examined these interactions from several perspectives. Carbon-aware freight-network planning and maritime EU ETS assessments address route configuration and policy implementation ( Kotzampasakis, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), while other studies evaluate compliance costs, modal shifts, allowance allocation, route choice, and incentive alignment ( Flodén et al., 2024; Sun Y. et al., 2024; Bucak et al., 2025). Hub-and-spoke network design and disruption analyses show that changes in connectivity can alter both operating costs and emissions ( Xu et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2024). Related port-cluster research further indicates that inter-port connectivity and coordinated development can shape the functional differentiation and structural evolution of regional port systems ( Li et al., 2026). Maritime allowance-allocation studies further demonstrate that regulatory design can influence carrier behavior and the distribution of abatement responsibilities ( Zhu et al., 2023; Shangguan et al., 2025). At the market level, allowance scarcity, price corridors, and Market Stability Reserve rules affect carbon-price expectations and abatement incentives ( Gerlagh et al., 2022; Pahle et al., 2025). Related research on shore-to-ship electricity also shows that the effectiveness of low-carbon support depends on the interaction between subsidy design and port competition ( Xu et al., 2025a).

Despite this progress, four research gaps remain. First, existing studies generally examine carbon-market regulation, shipping-network design, or clean-technology support separately, although these mechanisms interact in practice. Second, maritime optimization models commonly treat the allowance price as an exogenous scenario input and therefore omit the feedback from solved carrier emissions to the carbon-cost signal. Third, carrier-level emissions and EU-wide TNAC and MSR quantities operate at different scales; without an explicit conversion, their direct coupling may produce mechanically driven rather than economically interpretable outcomes. Fourth, policy evaluation requires repeatedly solving a discontinuous mixed-integer carrier-response model, yet the reliability of surrogate or heuristic search is rarely assessed against an exact benchmark.

To address these gaps, this study develops an AI-assisted bilevel Bayesian Optimization–Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (BO–MILP) framework. The upper layer is interpreted as a normative policy-design and decision-support proxy rather than a literal representation of the European Commission. It parameterizes a monotone emission-indexed support path, while the lower-level MILP determines the carrier’s network, vessel deployment, voyages, cargo flows, and compliance decisions. Solved carrier emissions are converted to sector-equivalent quantities and returned to a unit-consistent MAC–TNAC–MSR controller, which generates a feedback-adjusted, corridor-constrained carbon-cost signal. Gaussian-process BO is then used to search the discontinuous policy-response surface under a limited number of MILP evaluations.

This study makes three contributions. First, it establishes a scale-consistent and auditable feedback mechanism between carrier emissions and the carbon-cost signal without interpreting that signal as a market-clearing EU allowance price. Second, it integrates the policy signal with discrete carrier decisions while separately measuring physical emissions, ETS-covered emissions, private carrier cost, and policy-inclusive resource cost. Third, it validates BO through exhaustive enumeration of a structurally matched micro-instance and compares alternative algorithms under an identical evaluation budget. The framework thereby provides a transparent tool for evaluating the short-run emissions, cost, and operational implications of maritime support policies.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature, Sections 3 and 4 present the model and solution procedure, Section 5 reports the numerical results, and Sections 6 and 7 provide the discussion and conclusions. 2 Literature review

2.1 Evolution of carbon market mechanisms and price endogeneity

Carbon pricing mechanisms, particularly the EU ETS, have become central to maritime decarbonization research. Existing studies mainly examine allowance allocation, cost pass-through, and carbon leakage risks after shipping is brought within the ETS framework ( Gerlagh et al., 2022; Pahle et al., 2025). This stream clarifies how carbon costs are redistributed across carriers, routes, and trading partners once maritime transport is incorporated into an emissions trading regime. A related strand moves beyond static policy assessment and discusses the dynamic features of cap-and-trade systems, especially the role of reserve mechanisms and allowance scarcity in shaping carbon-price signals ( Tan et al., 2023). Viewed together, these studies indicate that the EU ETS is more than a regulatory surcharge: it is a market-based policy instrument that can influence strategic behavior across the shipping system.

Nevertheless, an important gap remains. Maritime applications commonly treat the allowance price as an external scenario input and therefore omit the computational feedback from carrier emissions to the allowance signal and back to network decisions. This study addresses that gap through a unit-consistent controller that maps solved carrier emissions to sector-equivalent quantities, updates the corridor-constrained MAC–TNAC–MSR signal, and resolves the carrier MILP until the annual emissions gap converges.

2.2 Shipping network topology and navigational decisions under carbon constraints

Under carbon constraints, strategic adjustment of shipping networks has become a central research theme. Existing studies can be grouped into three strands. The first examines route choice and speed optimization, emphasizing the trade-off between operating cost and emissions reduction ( Ye and Yuan, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). The second evaluates alternative fuels and their implications for network performance ( Zhang et al., 2025). The third investigates network reconfiguration, including the addition of transshipment ports to diversify risk, even when such adjustments may increase system-wide emissions ( Xu et al., 2021). These studies demonstrate that speed optimization significantly reduces fuel consumption, though it requires a trade-off with time-related costs ( Peng et al., 2024).

Within the maritime EU ETS literature, operational studies often examine partial adjustments such as rerouting to reduce regulated voyage exposure ( Sun L. et al., 2024). Fewer studies jointly determine hub selection, route opening, vessel deployment, and cargo-flow assignment. The lower-level MILP addresses this network-design gap, while the feedback controller returns the solved carrier response to the policy-signal module at a consistent sector scale ( Huang et al., 2022; Lynce de Faria, 2024; Monferdini et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025).

2.3 Hierarchical decision modeling of policy regulation and shipping response

Hierarchical models are widely used to represent sequential policy and firm decisions ( Uy et al., 2024). Recent studies examine incentive compatibility, maritime taxation, and multi-actor adjustment under carbon regulation ( Wang and Zhu, 2026), while bilevel formulations represent enterprise responses to policy constraints ( Zhu et al., 2023) and carbon-mitigation measures under explicit leader–follower structures ( Caruso et al., 2025). Related game-theoretic research in digital mobility shows how platform rules affect participation and welfare ( Guo and Xiao, 2026), providing cross-sector methodological evidence for rule-dependent operational response.

Such research commonly adopts a Stackelberg structure in which a policy designer precedes a carrier response ( Zhao et al., 2025). The general formulation records cap, support, investment, and leakage-control instruments discussed in related studies ( Liang et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Li, 2025; Martínez-Moya et al., 2025). The implemented main experiment is deliberately narrower: after a matched screening shows that the cap perturbation does not change the carrier solution, the active search is restricted to the emission-indexed support path.

2.4 Literature synthesis and methodological positioning

The literature suggests three requirements for a maritime ETS decision model. Carbon-pricing effects depend on credible policy and available adjustment channels ( Döbbeling-Hildebrandt et al., 2024), while shipping decarbonization requires coordinated technological and operational change ( Müller-Casseres et al., 2024). Network studies further show that hub location, deployment, transshipment, and green-technology decisions interact ( Zhen et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022), consistent with operational evidence on fleet deployment and technology adoption ( Shahriari et al., 2016; Kleinert et al., 2021). Cross-sector low-carbon scheduling research likewise demonstrates the value of integrating technology and operational decisions ( Xiao Y. et al., 2026).

Accordingly, the paper develops an AI-assisted policy-response architecture in which the main experiment searches a monotone support path, the carrier MILP resolves discrete network and deployment decisions, and the feedback controller returns solved emissions to the MAC–TNAC–MSR signal at a consistent sector scale.

3.5 Model linearization strategy

The implemented lower level evaluates fuel burn at an economic-speed anchor, leaving voyage frequency as the principal operating variable. This local approximation keeps each policy evaluation within a MILP.

3.5.1 Fixed-speed linearization

For each vessel class, the sailing speed is fixed at an economic cruising anchor ( Equation 37):

The approximation is deliberately local: it is intended to represent the cruising regime around normal liner-service speeds, not the full continuous speed-control problem.

3.6 Feedback-coupled policy–response mapping

The model is summarized as a feedback-coupled policy-response mapping from an upper-level policy vector theta to a solved carrier response x*(theta). For each candidate, the controller produces a carbon-cost signal, the carrier MILP returns discrete network and compliance decisions, and the solved emissions are mapped back to sector scale. Binary hub, route, and vessel decisions make this mapping discontinuous.

The resulting upper-level response is discontinuous because hub, route, vessel, and voyage decisions change discretely. Bayesian optimization is therefore used as a sample-efficient outer search, and an exhaustive micro-instance provides an independent accuracy benchmark.

4 Solution algorithm

4.1 Bilevel solution framework

The bilevel model in Section 3 is computationally hard because the lower-level carrier response contains binary hub-selection, route-opening, and vessel-deployment variables, integer voyage-frequency decisions, multi-commodity flow constraints, and capacity coupling. Even without the upper-level policy search, this lower-level problem generalizes capacitated hub location and fixed-charge network design, both of which are NP-hard. The upper-level objective is therefore an expensive black-box value function generated by repeatedly solving a discrete network MILP.

A standard KKT reformulation is not applicable because the lower level contains binary and integer decisions. The implemented method therefore evaluates candidate policies through nested BO and MILP solves.

The proposed BO-MILP strategy treats the upper-level policy path as an expensive black-box design problem. Each candidate is scored only after the feedback-coupled carrier MILP has converged, so the surrogate learns the realized emissions and resource-cost response of the discrete network rather than a reduced-form proxy. 6 Discussion

The results demonstrate how an emission-indexed support policy can influence short-run carrier operations under a corridor-constrained carbon-cost signal. Relative to the matched nine-hub baseline, the representative best-evaluated policy reduces cumulative physical emissions from 36.887 to 26.414 ktCO2 , corresponding to a 28.39% reduction. ETS-covered emissions decrease from 9.501 to 6.371 ktCO2 , or 32.94%. Private carrier cost falls by 0.287%, whereas resource cost increases by only 0.213% after EUR 2.532 million of discounted support expenditure is included. The same-constraint physical-emission minimization yields a 33.05% attainable reduction, indicating that the representative policy captures 85.91% of the modeled short-run abatement potential.

The carbon-cost results clarify the role and limitations of the MAC–TNAC–MSR feedback mechanism. After solved carrier emissions are converted to sector-equivalent quantities and returned to the controller, the representative policy converges in two iterations to 75.0, 85.0, and 86.7 EUR/tCO2 for 2024–2026. The first two values reach the imposed corridor ceilings, whereas the 2026 value lies within the corresponding corridor. The signal should therefore be interpreted as a feedback-adjusted and corridor-constrained carbon-cost signal rather than an empirically estimated or market-clearing EUA price. Its value lies in consistently transmitting changes in modeled emissions to the carrier’s compliance and operational decisions.

The matched cap-only diagnostic produces the same carrier solution as the baseline, indicating that the tested cap adjustment is inactive within the current operating range. The observed emission reduction is instead associated with the emission-indexed support path and the resulting redistribution of voyages among available fixed-fuel vessels. This distinction is important because Figure 7 represents solved voyage deployment shares rather than fleet conversion or technology penetration. The results consequently describe an operational response within the existing fleet and network, not rapid fleet-wide adoption of LNG, methanol, or other alternative fuels.

The exact micro-instance provides independent evidence on the computational value of BO. Exhaustive evaluation of all 248 feasible policies establishes the exact optimum, against which BO and four alternative search methods are assessed under the same initialization, lower-level oracle, 30 seeds, and 20-evaluation budget. BO achieves a 0.00% median optimality gap, a 4.35% mean gap, and an 80.0% exact-hit rate, whereas the competing methods produce substantially larger mean gaps. These findings support BO as a sample-efficient approach for searching a discontinuous policy-response surface when each policy evaluation requires solving a mixed-integer carrier model. They do not imply universal superiority over all deterministic or heuristic methods.

Several limitations define the interpretation of the findings. The case represents one normalized carrier over a short 2024–2026 horizon, with fixed demand, vessel fuel types, speed anchors, and network topology across the principal comparisons. Part of the OD matrix is constructed for the controlled case, and the carrier-to-sector conversion remains a calibrated representation rather than a complete multi-carrier allowance-market model. Moreover, exact outer-level optimality is established for the micro-instance, while the main Asia–Europe case reports the best policy identified within the available BO evaluation budget.

Future research could extend the framework to multiple interacting carriers and a sector-scale allowance market calibrated with observed carrier shares and TNAC–MSR data. Endogenous fuel choice, fleet renewal, slow steaming, fuel availability, methane slip, life-cycle emissions, demand response, and port congestion could also be incorporated. These extensions would allow the framework to evaluate longer-term technology transitions and policy robustness under market, fuel-price, and demand uncertainty.

7 Conclusion

This study develops an AI-assisted bilevel BO–MILP framework for analyzing the interaction between an emission-indexed support policy, a feedback-adjusted carbon-cost signal, and discrete carrier network responses under the maritime EU ETS. The framework distinguishes physical emissions, ETS-covered emissions, private carrier cost, policy expenditure, and resource cost, while feeding solved carrier emissions back to a unit-consistent MAC–TNAC–MSR controller.

In the Asia–Europe case, the representative best-evaluated policy reduces physical emissions by 28.39% and ETS-covered emissions by 32.94% relative to a matched nine-hub baseline, while increasing resource cost by 0.213%. It captures 85.91% of the same-constraint short-run abatement potential. The matched cap-only diagnostic produces no change, indicating that the modeled improvement is associated with support-induced voyage deployment among fixed-fuel vessels rather than cap tightening or fleet conversion. The resulting 75.0/85.0/86.7 EUR/tCO2 path is interpreted as a corridor-constrained model signal rather than an EU-wide market-clearing allowance price.

Exact enumeration of the 248-policy micro-instance further shows that BO can identify high-quality policies with a limited number of lower-level MILP evaluations. Under a common 20-evaluation budget, BO achieves a 0.00% median gap and an 80.0% exact-hit rate across 30 seeds. The framework therefore provides a transparent and sample-efficient decision-support tool for assessing short-run maritime policy responses, while its conclusions remain conditional on the specified demand, fleet, network, and policy settings.
