title: How BCD Supports Corporates to Decarbonise Business Travel | Sustainability Magazine
description:
How can corporate travel managers distinguish between genuine net-zero strategies and superficial offset schemes when evaluating travel suppliers?
Corporate travel buyers have an opportunity to drive more sustainable practices across the travel industry, so how you build it into your procurement is key.
The Global Business Travel Association (GBTA) has some great procurement toolkits that can help corporates ask the right questions and then assess them in a meaningful way.
What single policy or technology breakthrough will most accelerate corporate travel decarbonisation over the next 3–5 years?
In terms of Scope 3, we have been able to make significant progress in decarbonising our own business travel.
text:
In an era where sustainability is no longer a corporate "nice-to-have" but a fundamental business imperative, the expectation of travel management has evolved significantly.

As organisations strive to reconcile business growth with climate responsibility, the challenge lies in balancing essential travel with meaningful emission reductions.

Olivia Ruggles-Brise, Vice President of Sustainability at BCD Travel, suggests that the corporate travel sector can serve as a vital cross-sector testing ground for wider sustainability strategies, highlighting the power of embedding carbon awareness directly into everyday decision-making.

The sector can both leverage data-driven insights to influence traveller behaviour and explore cross-industry partnerships that champion sustainable aviation fuels.

Olivia was speaking ahead of her appearance on the Global Decarbonisation Strategies panel at Sustainability LIVE: The London Summit, which takes place 8-9 September. Get your tickets here.

How does BCD help corporate clients define 'essential' purposeful travel to achieve 'travelling smarter, not less' without impacting business growth?

For me, purposeful travel starts with a very simple question: what value does this trip create that cannot be achieved another way? That means being intentional about when we travel, how we travel and what outcome we expect from it.

Companies need sustainability to work alongside cost control, duty of care and traveller experience, not compete with them. We help clients look at travel through that business lens: the purpose of the trip, stakeholder value, cost, traveller wellbeing, carbon impact and available alternatives.

That allows organisations to protect the trips that matter most while identifying areas where a different mode, cabin, meeting format or policy approach may deliver the same outcome with lower emissions and often lower cost.

The strongest programmes are not anti-travel; they are pro-value.

How is BCD updating its reporting architecture to ensure enterprise clients receive audited, defensible carbon data that stands up to scrutiny?

The advantage of a managed travel programme is that travel data is all stored in one place and, as such, BCD has offered robust emissions reporting for travel programmes for many years.

Many organisations have corporate sustainability goals, but translating those goals into travel-specific reporting and action is still where complexity often sits.

As new regulations put the spotlight on data quality and calculation methodologies, and with the opportunities offered by AI, we are evolving our reporting platform to include built-in audit tokens, whereby each data point can be traced back to source data.

This allows for different calculation methodologies to be used and the ability to include emissions data from expense reports as well.

How does BCD use messaging and behavioural nudges to guide employees toward lower-emission choices?

Traveller behaviour is critical because the booking moment is where many decisions are actually made. Policies and targets matter, but if sustainability information appears too late, it is much harder for travellers to act on it.

We also know that traveller communication on sustainable choices is still inconsistent across many programmes, which makes point-of-booking guidance even more important.

BCD’s approach is to bring relevant sustainability cues into the tools travellers already use, including our own booking tool Tripsource, and other supported online booking environments. This can include CO₂ visibility, comparisons, methodology selection, hotel sustainability information, carbon-fee display and nudges that make lower-emission options easier to understand, such as when a train might be a viable alternative to a flight.

Carbon fees can be especially powerful because they show the total cost of a trip, beyond the ticket price. By assigning a cost to emissions, organisations can make environmental impact more visible and encourage better decisions at the point of choice.

When clients need deeper support, we have specialist communications consultants within Advito, the consulting arm of BCD, who can help design traveller engagement campaigns and messaging strategies grounded in programme goals.

Real change happens when the better choice is visible, practical and aligned with the business purpose of the trip.

At Sustainability LIVE, you're sharing the stage with leaders from other sectors. What cross-sector lessons can non-travel industries learn from corporate travel's approach to decarbonisation?

First of all, most large companies undertake business travel, so on a practical level it is a key lever for their own decarbonisation actions. While the proportion of a company’s emissions from travel will vary, it is often one of the most controllable scope 3 categories and one where employees can also get involved.

One of the most valuable lessons corporate travel can offer other sectors is that decarbonisation works best when it is embedded into everyday decisions, not managed as a separate sustainability project.

Travel programmes already connect policy, data, suppliers, technology, budgets and human behaviour. This makes them a useful testbed for practical decarbonisation: you can measure impact, influence choices and adjust policy in a relatively direct way.

At the same time, while embedding sustainability into a travel programme is key, ultimately decarbonisation of travel is down to the airlines and hotels that provide the travel products. Corporate travel has a vital role in driving decarbonisation across these sectors through consolidating and prioritising demand for low-carbon alternatives, for example through investing in Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

How do you work with hotel supply chains and rail operators to ensure corporate travellers have viable, low-carbon alternatives at booking?

The Advito Hotel Sustainability Index uses data provided by the hotel to give each property a score out of 100, based on factors such as carbon emissions, energy and water consumption, renewable energy and eco-certifications.

The top 2-3% of hotels in each city/region are also identified as a “greener choice”. This score can be shown in our booking platform, helping travellers compare properties and identify stronger sustainability performers without having to search separately

Integrating rail into corporate booking platforms is complex because content, availability and booking integration vary by market, but we are working to expand our coverage annually.

But where rail is a viable alternative to air, particularly on shorter routes, it can play an important role. Through our involvement with the Travalyst Coalition, we are also collaborating on an industry-wide methodology to calculate rail emissions.

For ground transport, the message is similar: make better options easy to find. EVs and hybrid vehicles are generally visible on all car rental platforms, but we also need to avoid oversimplifying the issue.

A smaller, efficient petrol car can still be a better choice than a large SUV. Ultimately, the goal is not to overwhelm travellers with sustainability data. It is to make credible alternatives visible, comparable and practical when decisions are being made.

How can corporate travel managers distinguish between genuine net-zero strategies and superficial offset schemes when evaluating travel suppliers?

My first piece of advice would be to treat all claims with a level of scepticism. Even the most robust strategies might use different definitions, or the priorities may not be aligned with your own. Corporate travel buyers have an opportunity to drive more sustainable practices across the travel industry, so how you build it into your procurement is key.

First of all, it’s vital to be clear on your own priorities – is it carbon emissions, waste reduction, progress or measurement? The Global Business Travel Association (GBTA) has some great procurement toolkits that can help corporates ask the right questions and then assess them in a meaningful way.

On the hotel side, you can ask for progress against science-based targets and some of the large chains such as Radisson and IHG have robust net zero or low carbon hotel programmes. However, the number of properties achieving this level of accreditation is still very low.

When it comes to aviation, there are a number of industry pathways towards net-zero, but there are also increasing questions as to the viability of those pathways.

Many airlines are investing in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and should be able to share data with their clients on where and when this fuel is used and provide corporates with the opportunity to purchase the scope 3 credits.

Carbon removals are increasingly playing a role in aviation and you should ask your airline partners how they are building this into their strategy. CORSIA is the aviation industry’s offset programme that is coming into force in a phased way. Essentially, it uses accredited offsets so that growth is carbon neutral from 2019 levels.

All in all, the journey to net zero in corporate travel is really complicated. There are many different standards and providers which can sometimes lead to a confusing and overwhelming position.

What single policy or technology breakthrough will most accelerate corporate travel decarbonisation over the next 3–5 years?

Corporate travel’s ability to decarbonise is closely tied to aviation decarbonisation. We are still a long way from a net-zero aviation industry, but in the near term, SAF is one of the most realistic levers available for reducing flight-related emissions.

Interest in SAF is growing, but adoption remains limited today. Scaling supply, improving corporate access and creating clear accounting frameworks will be critical over the next few years. SAF use doubled in 2025, but it still represents less than 1% of total jet fuel.

Government mandates, as we are seeing in the EU, UK and Singapore, are helping drive demand, but they need to be supported by incentives and policy stability across the value chain, such as the UK’s revenue certainty mechanism.

Corporate travel has a vital role to play in sending demand signals that can then stimulate production and supply. Of course, the single policy breakthrough that could make a huge difference is modernising how we manage airspace, particularly in Europe.

According to the European Commission, air traffic management delays and inefficiencies led to 11.6 million tonnes of excess CO₂ in 2019. The opportunity is significant, although the political barriers remain difficult to overcome.

Regarding BCD Travel's emissions reduction targets, where have the best opportunities to lower Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions occurred and what remains toughest to decarbonise?

As a services company, our Scope 1 and 2 emissions are very small, but we have been able to make real progress in terms of purchasing renewable energy across our office estate and electrifying our company fleet.

Since our 2019 baseline, we have reduced our Scope 1 and 2 emissions by over 73%.

In terms of Scope 3, we have been able to make significant progress in decarbonising our own business travel. As with many companies, it is in our supply chain that the most opportunity, but also the most challenges, lie.

However, we are finding the key to making real progress is having good data from suppliers, particularly on the tech side.

As a largely remote company, we report our “working from home emissions”. One of our greatest challenges is how we measure this in a meaningful way that can reflect colleagues’ own actions to decarbonise their home offices.

I’d love to hear from people who are also tackling this challenge.

Olivia was speaking ahead of her appearance on the Global Decarbonisation Strategies panel at Sustainability LIVE: The London Summit, which takes place 8-9 September. Get your tickets here.

text:
RevaTerra, an advanced materials company engineering natural residuals into industrial-grade bioenergy products, on Nov. 11 announced the final close of an oversubscribed $1.265 million seed financing.

The round was led by BlueLake.vc through investments from BL.vc Deep Tech and BlueLake Syndications alongside mission-aligned private investors. RevaTerra will use the proceeds to expand customer and manufacturing relationships, advance product development, and grow its team.

RevaTerra develops proprietary formulations that upgrade forestry and agricultural residuals into high-performance materials for industrial applications. Using advanced biomass characterization and machine learning, the company tailors those formulations to the specific feedstock a producer is running, addressing the variability that has long limited consistency in biomass-derived products.

“This financing marks an important milestone for RevaTerra as we move from technical validation into commercial execution,” said Jude Davies, co-founder and CEO of RevaTerra. “With this support, we can expand our customer programs and manufacturing relationships, continue advancing our technology, and bring our products into broader commercial use.”

“Global energy demand is rising faster than the system can adapt, creating one of the decade’s largest infrastructure investment opportunities,” says James Rutledge, partner at BlueLake.vc. “RevaTerra’s high-performance biofuel can scale globally using abundant domestic feedstocks while delivering more energy per unit than coal. By enabling existing coal-fired power plants to transition without costly retrofits, it offers a faster, more capital-efficient path to meeting surging power demand. We believe this combination of economics, energy security, and scalability positions RevaTerra to deliver significant long-term value."

RevaTerra's patent-pending Arcana formulation delivers a high-performance white pellet engineered for industrial energy applications. The company works with industrial energy users and materials producers facing growing demand for reliable, lower-carbon inputs, a need intensified by rising power consumption and tightening emissions requirements across the United States, Europe, and Asia.

"Most approaches to upgrading biomass require significant capital commitment," said Joe Napier, PhD, co-founder and CTO of RevaTerra. "We took a different path. Our formulations achieve high-performance levels using existing production pipelines and the operating conditions producers already use. That is what makes the technology deployable now rather than years from now."

The company’s focus on near-term deployment has shaped RevaTerra’s commercial strategy, allowing producers to improve performance without replacing existing infrastructure or fundamentally changing how they operate.

“RevaTerra’s ability to improve performance through existing manufacturing and energy infrastructure gives the company a compelling path to scale,” said Chris Cesareo, partner at BlueLake.vc. “RevaTerra addresses critical bottlenecks to biofuel adoption such as storage stability, energy density, and unit economics, unlocking opportunities for rapid market expansion.”

The closing follows a series of technical and commercial milestones, including successful production trials on commercial pellet-manufacturing equipment and independent testing, demonstrating strong energy density, durability, and handling characteristics. RevaTerra’s Angel investors, Advisors, and Board have also played an important role, providing the insight, experience, and backing that helped the company reach these milestones.

Gunderson Dettmer Stough Villeneuve Franklin & Hachigian, LLP served as legal counsel to RevaTerra in connection with the financing, and Hutchison PLLC served as legal counsel to BlueLake.vc.

text:
Boomtown is set to have a main stage fuelled entirely by UK-produced green hydrogen.

The stage at the Hampshire festival uses generators that create electricity via hydrogen fuel cells and self-charging Hydrogen Power Unit (HPU) batteries.

The by-products are water and heat only, meaning zero carbon emissions, fumes, or loud diesel noise, organisers said.

"We are really keen to pioneer sustainability," said Poppy Handy, the festival's operations director.

The stage, HydroXL, opened on Friday and its arena can hold up to 20,000 people.

"We started last year working with a hydrogen company on a smaller scale," Handy said.

"This is brand-new technology for the festival industry so we started smaller, we found it worked.

"Now we have doubled our efforts with it being a main stage."

The adult-only festival is this year hosting 77,000, its largest attendance yet.

But with a heat warning across the South and a drought affecting the region, it has faced issues with dust.

This is partly due to the festival being based in the South Downs, which has lots of limestone and chalk areas.

Boomtown has warned festivalgoers to take precautions like bringing face coverings, wearing sunscreen, and staying hydrated.

"We've thought very carefully about fire risks and increased provisions," Handy said.

"Our top priority is to make sure the people of Boomtown are safe."

There has also been a ban on camping stoves and barbecues.

In the past seven years the festival's organisers said it had reduced its carbon footprint by 98%.

It also features initiatives like The Repairium - bringing once loved items and repairing them - like trolleys or instruments.

And Energy Garden has set up a tent to teach people how to solder their own solar panels from scratch.

text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is not a single compound like conventional Jet A-1. It is a blend of traditional fuel with components derived from diverse sustainable feedstocks, including fats, oils, alcohols, or pyrolysis products.

For lab personnel, this diversity creates a critical analytical challenge: a changing fuel matrix.

While final blends currently use low percentages of SAF, it's imperative to accurately measure the sustainable blend components before they are added to the Jet A-1. This is where the matrix change is most impactful, and the requirement for accurate analysis is highest.

Key Considerations of Sustainable Aviation Fuel Analysis

Routine elemental analysis (e.g., measuring sulfur, chlorine, or metals) relies on the assumption of a consistent hydrocarbon matrix. Introducing sustainable components requires careful consideration of two primary factors:

Oxygen Interference: Feedstocks derived from biogenic sources introduce significant oxygen into the sample. Oxygen is a strong X-ray absorber. If your XRF analyzer is calibrated only on a conventional mineral oil matrix, the oxygen in the SAF component will absorb the X-rays used to measure elements like sulfur, leading to a low bias (a lower-than-expected result). Depending on the sample type, matrix matching—calibrating with standards that closely mimic the sample’s composition—is required to obtain accurate values.

Contaminant Risk: Waste-derived feedstocks can introduce trace interfering elements (chlorine, silicon, phosphorus) that must be precisely measured to prevent engine damage or meet final jet fuel specifications.

description:
The government of Brazil on Aug. 12 published a decree that establishes rules and regulations for the country’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandate, formally referred to as the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program (ProBioQAV).
ProBioQAV was formally established by Brazil’s Fuel of the Future Law in October 2024.
Notably, the program includes a book-and-claim chain-of-custody model that allows the physical product and its environmental attributes to be traded by different commercial operations and purchasers.

The government of Brazil on Aug. 12 published a decree that establishes rules and regulations for the country’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandate, formally referred to as the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program (ProBioQAV).

ProBioQAV was formally established by Brazil’s Fuel of the Future Law in October 2024. The program requires domestic airline operators to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions starting with a 1% reduction in 2027 and scaling up to a 10% reduction in 2037. Notably, the program includes a book-and-claim chain-of-custody model that allows the physical product and its environmental attributes to be traded by different commercial operations and purchasers.

Under the newly announced regulations, the carbon intensity (CI) of SAF can be determined during the REnovaBio carbon intensity calculation tool or the ICAO CORISA methodology.

According to the decree, Brazil’s National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (ANP) and the National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC) are to issue complementary regulations necessary to implement the SAF mandate by Dec. 18, 2026.

text:
The regenerative advantage: Sustainable Aviation Fuel and the new power geography of the Indo-Pacific

Renewable fuels change the logic of energy security

In the aviation context, SAF offers a fundamentally different approach to the energy security challenge, as it changes the logic of fuel production itself. Conventional fuels derive their value from finite geological reserves that must be extracted, transported, and invariably, depleted. Renewable fuels can instead be produced from feedstocks that are continually replenished through biological and cyclical processes, including agricultural wastes and low-value by-products, forestry residues, municipal waste streams, and regenerative crops.

The Indo-Pacific’s feedstock advantage

The Indo-Pacific is often discussed through the lens of its energy vulnerabilities. Many countries in the region remain heavily dependent on imported fuels, whilst growing populations and expanding middle classes continue to drive rising demand for aviation, shipping, and regional connectivity. Yet, these same characteristics that are driving demand also point toward a longer-term opportunity, albeit one that requires time, sustained investment, policy support, and regional partnerships to be fully realised.

Yet feedstock abundance does not automatically translate into fuel supply. Building the processing infrastructure, expertise, and certification frameworks needed to convert these resources into renewable fuels can take several years. Across much of the Indo-Pacific, those value chains are nascent, and aviation demand is growing faster than the domestic capacity to serve it with cleaner fuels. This creates a unique opportunity for regional cooperation, investment, and industrial development, including in Australia.

From a timing standpoint, Australia is not the only country eyeing this opportunity and the window to emerge as a regional leader in this space will not stay open indefinitely. Singapore, which has little domestic feedstock of its own, has moved fastest on policy, establishing a mandatory SAF levy from October 2026 that will fund a 1 per cent SAF uplift this year, rising to 3–5 per cent by 2030. Meanwhile, Japan has paired a SAF mandate for 2030 with its own domestic production incentives, South Korea’s 1 per cent blending requirements will take effect in 2027, and India will also introduce a 1 per cent mandate for international flights in 2027, scaling to 5 per cent by 2030.

However, most of these markets are natural importers, not producers. Singapore, Japan, and South Korea have limited domestic feedstock and are certain to rely on imported SAF to meet their targets, whilst Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam are better placed to become net exporters by the 2040s, based on the size of their agricultural sectors. Australia’s opportunity, in turn, is not to out-produce these latter markets on volume, but to become a reliable, geographically proximate supplier and technical partner to the region’s importers.

Western Australia’s role

Australia has a unique position within this emerging landscape, and Western Australia (WA) sits at the centre of this opportunity. The state’s abundant renewable energy resources, established export infrastructure, and geographic proximity to some of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets – many of which lack the domestic infrastructure to convert their own feedstock resources – makes it well placed to help fill the Indo-Pacific’s emerging SAF supply gap. WA, and Australia more broadly, has the extensive agricultural capability, renewable energy resources, land availability, and export infrastructure needed to do so at scale. A mature Australian low-carbon liquid fuels industry could be worth $36 billion and cut cumulative emissions by 230 million tonnes of CO2 by 2050.

This combination of geography, urgency, and resource endowment is now attracting serious policy attention. The Australian Government’s $1.1 billion Cleaner Fuels Program, a 10-year production incentive for the domestic low carbon liquid fuels industry, signals a national commitment to the development of this industry. The 2026-27 Federal Budget went further still, by foreshadowing a local demand-side measure (e.g. a legally binding mandate for SAF supply at Australian airports). If ratified, this would provide revenue certainty for local SAF production, which remains one of the critical enablers for new developments to become bankable.

Closer to home, the Cook Government’s $1.2 million WA Advanced Biofuels Strategy, due for delivery in the second half of 2026, is mapping the state’s feedstock potential. As one might expect, Western Australia is home to a wide range of potential renewable inputs, spanning oat, wheat, and barley residues, regenerative woody biomass from mallees and blue gums, as well as canola feedstocks.

The regenerative advantage

Stepping back, the most important difference between fossil fuels and renewable fuels is that they reward fundamentally different behaviours. The former system has historically rewarded countries fortunate enough to sit atop concentrated reserves of oil. The emerging renewable fuel economy increasingly rewards those capable of maintaining the ecosystems, agricultural systems, and waste management networks that enable continual resource renewal.

Such ‘natural capital’ should therefore be recognised as a strategic asset, with soil productivity, water security, biodiversity, and landscape health all serving as critical inputs that directly influence future fuel production. The countries that recognise this relationship earliest will be best positioned to shape the next chapter of regional energy security. For Australia, realising that role will also be a function of policy design, which will need to align domestic supply obligations with export ambition, ensuring that its capacity to be a regional partner works in tandem with meeting its own local needs.

Nonetheless, Western Australia, and Australia more broadly, has the opportunity to help define a new model of resilience for the Indo-Pacific. In a world where strategic advantage has historically flowed from the control of finite resources, the future of energy security may increasingly belong to those capable of continually regenerating them.

text:
Developing Brazil’s green hydrogen market is strategically important worldwide. It has attracted significant foreign investment, but the sector must still overcome bottlenecks before it can expand in the country. That was the assessment of experts participating in the livestream “Green Hydrogen: Promise, Strategic Bet or Hype?” on Tuesday (11). The event is part of the Energy Transition project, organized by Valor and O Globo.

The latest foreign investments were announced in June by the European Union, which plans to invest 3 million in the development of nine green hydrogen projects in Brazil. The investments are being made through the H2Uppp program, implemented by the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ).

Isabela Santos, coordinator of H2Uppp Brazil, explained that the nine projects are in addition to eight other initiatives supported by the organization in the country. In addition to connecting the projects with Europe’s private sector, the organization provides them with technical assistance.

The companies receiving support operate throughout the green hydrogen value chain, from production to fuel consumption.

The initiatives include the development of e-methanol—or green methanol, produced by combining green hydrogen and CO₂—sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a biofuel that replaces conventional jet fuel, and projects to decarbonize the automotive sector. “Our work is to support and expand the green hydrogen market. We already operate in nine countries, but Brazil is highly strategic,” Santos said.

The nine new projects that will receive European investment are expected to be announced during European Hydrogen Week, held in Brussels, Belgium, in October. The list includes projects to establish green corridors between European and Brazilian ports for exports of green hydrogen, ammonia and green steel.

Meeting foreign demand for green hydrogen is strategically important, but the domestic market also offers enormous potential, noted Paulo Emilio Valadão de Miranda, a professor at Coppe-UFRJ and president of the Brazilian Hydrogen Association (ABH2).

An association study mapped 34 projects underway in Brazil with projected annual production of up to 4.6 million tonnes of low-emission hydrogen beginning in 2035, compared with expected annual demand of approximately 3.7 million tonnes over the same period.

The projects mapped include five initiatives to develop domestic production and consumption with support from the Ministry of Mines and Energy. Some are led by major companies such as CSN and Petrobras.

In addition, 95% of the projects mapped by ABH2 also plan to produce ammonia from green hydrogen. The ammonia could be exported for use by the shipping sector or used domestically to produce fertilizers, which are in high demand in Brazil but have risen sharply in price since the conflict between Russia and Ukraine began.

Another opportunity is using green hydrogen to decarbonize products that Brazil already exports. One example, according to Miranda, is iron ore. Companies including Vale and Green Energy Park (GEP) are already working on the direct reduction of iron ore using hydrogen.

Besides increasing the value added of the final exported product, the process makes steel more competitive, particularly in Europe, which has stringent policies taxing goods that use fossil fuels in production.

“This can be done with other products, which means strengthening the domestic market, reindustrializing the country and attracting foreign investment. It is a strategy that benefits Brazil and the environment while also helping decarbonize countries that lack the necessary production capacity and therefore need to import hydrogen or decarbonized products,” Miranda said.

Despite Brazil’s immense potential in the sector, given its availability of raw materials and energy sources for producing low-carbon hydrogen, cost remains one of the main bottlenecks. The primary production method is water electrolysis, a process that uses electricity to separate water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. The problem is its high production cost, ranging from R$10 to R$70 per kilogram.

Miranda believes investment must be expanded in initiatives using other methods, such as biomass, which costs between R$7 and R$20 per kilogram. One project in this area is supported by the H2Uppp program. It uses pig waste from the region of Toledo, Paraná, as the raw material for SAF production. The waste previously posed a risk of phosphate contamination to the region’s soil and groundwater.

“The bottleneck is finding buyers inside and outside Brazil so that production can increase and reduce the cost of green hydrogen and synthetic fuels—which require hydrogen in their production. Projects in Brazil have taken off in recent years. There was hype, but we are now left with the crème de la crème: those who want to do business in this sector will do so,” Santos said.

The Energy Transition project is sponsored by Vale.

text: Europe has pulled ahead of the US and Asia on cleaner jet fuel adoption, largely because regulation is forcing airlines to buy it while others rely on voluntary incentives. Under the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation rule, airlines must blend 2% sustainable aviation fuel starting in 2025, with targets rising to 70% by 2050. That mandate is driving real uptake. In 2023 SAF made up just 0.17% of global jet fuel, but European carriers accounted for the bulk of it. DHL Group alone used more SAF than all US airlines combined, and FedEx bought none despite a pledge to hit 30% by 2030. Industry analysts say the EU approach provides a real stick, while the US sticks to tax credits and goals without requirements, leaving a gap between net-zero pledges and actual purchases. The lead comes even as Europe faces tighter conventional jet fuel supplies. Decades of refinery closures have left the bloc importing about 30-40% of its jet fuel, half of that historically via the Strait of Hormuz. Energy Aspects estimated a nearly 600,000 bpd deficit for Europe in Q3 2026, versus surpluses of 116,000 bpd in the US and 425,000 bpd in Asia-Pacific, with stocks covering less than 30 days of demand. To keep planes flying, Europe has ramped imports from the US, Canada, Nigeria, India and South Korea, and boosted refinery runs. The Commission is also pushing faster SAF and synthetic fuel scale-up to cut Middle East dependence, while monitoring stocks and allowing temporary use of US Jet A grade. Airlines complain the mandates raise costs and put them at a disadvantage to Asian and Gulf carriers, but regulators say the rules are needed to decarbonize aviation and reduce oil reliance. - World Business News.

title: How Kenyan businesses can turn sustainability into competitive advantage as climate risks rise
description:
In 2026, companies are facing growing pressure from investors, customers, regulators and financial institutions to address climate risks while remaining competitive.
For businesses, the challenge is no longer simply making sustainability commitments.
It is finding practical ways to reduce environmental impact, strengthen resilience and turn emerging opportunities into commercial value.
Sustainable aviation fuel offers a way to reduce the carbon intensity of existing operations while new technologies continue to develop.The scale of Kenya’s aviation-fuel demand makes the project particularly significant.
Sustainability is becoming part of how businesses manage risk, attract investment and plan for growth.
text:
21

By Gabriella Wanjiru Kiarie

Sustainability is rapidly moving from the margins of corporate strategy to the centre of business decisions. In 2026, companies are facing growing pressure from investors, customers, regulators and financial institutions to address climate risks while remaining competitive. For businesses, the challenge is no longer simply making sustainability commitments. It is finding practical ways to reduce environmental impact, strengthen resilience and turn emerging opportunities into commercial value.

Kenya’s financial sector provides a clear example of this shift. Standard Chartered Bank Kenya has continued expanding its sustainable-finance portfolio, with more than KSh97 billion mobilized since 2021 for areas including renewable energy, sustainable infrastructure, affordable housing and women-led businesses. The development highlights the growing role of financial institutions in directing capital towards projects that support environmental and social objectives.This matters because access to finance can determine whether businesses are able to invest in cleaner technology, energy efficiency and more resilient operations.

Kenya Airways and the move towards sustainable aviation -The transition is also reaching industries where reducing emissions is particularly difficult.On 12 May 2026, Kenya Airways and Rubis Energy Kenya signed an agreement in Nairobi to develop a proposed US$70.5 million–US$82.2 million sustainable aviation fuel refinery. The facility is expected to produce around 32,000 tonnes of SAF annually, using locally available waste oils and animal fats as feedstock.The project addresses a major challenge for aviation: aircraft cannot simply be replaced with zero-emission alternatives in the short term.

Sustainable aviation fuel offers a way to reduce the carbon intensity of existing operations while new technologies continue to develop.The scale of Kenya’s aviation-fuel demand makes the project particularly significant. Kenya Airways estimates that Jomo Kenyatta International Airport consumes around 2.9 million litres of jet fuel every day.The proposed refinery also demonstrates how environmental challenges can create new commercial opportunities. Waste materials that would otherwise have limited value could become inputs for a new fuel industry, creating potential economic activity alongside environmental benefits.

Climate change is increasingly being treated as a business risk rather than simply an environmental concern.Droughts can affect agricultural production, flooding can disrupt infrastructure and changing weather patterns can place pressure on supply chains. For businesses, these disruptions can translate directly into higher costs, lost revenue and operational delays.Companies can respond by assessing climate risks, diversifying suppliers, improving resource efficiency and investing in infrastructure that can withstand disruption.The businesses best prepared for these changes are likely to be those that treat environmental risks as part of wider financial and operational planning.

The strongest sustainability strategies are not simply about reducing emissions. They can also improve efficiency, open new markets and strengthen competitiveness.Businesses can reduce costs through lower energy and water consumption, use renewable energy to improve energy resilience, and develop products and services for growing markets such as clean transport, sustainable agriculture, recycling and renewable energy.The Kenya Airways-Rubis project illustrates this approach particularly well: a challenge facing the aviation industry is being approached as an opportunity to develop a new local industry.

As sustainability becomes more closely linked to finance and corporate decision-making, evidence is becoming increasingly important.Businesses need reliable information on areas such as emissions, energy use, waste, water consumption and climate-related risks. Setting measurable targets allows companies to demonstrate progress and identify where further investment is needed.For companies operating in Kenya, the direction of travel is clear. Sustainability is becoming part of how businesses manage risk, attract investment and plan for growth.

As sustainability becomes a defining factor in investment, competitiveness and long-term survival, the real question is: will businesses lead the transition—or wait until the cost of falling behind becomes impossible to ignore?

text:
Montana Renewables has cleared a major milestone in sustainable aviation fuel production. The company finished its MaxSAF 150 expansion at Great Falls, Montana, on schedule in early May 2026, pushing total SAF capacity to 150 million gallons a year. That number lands at a pointed moment, with airlines and regulators both hunting for dependable, large-scale clean fuel sources. Parent company Calumet confirmed the plant is now fully operational following a planned turnaround.

Calumet president and CEO Todd Borgmann laid out the timeline without much fanfare. "We brought down Montana Renewables for a turnaround in MaxSAF 150 expansion in early March and successfully commenced operations in early May," he said. Packed into that two-month window: mechanical upgrades, catalyst conditioning, and the kind of performance validation work that determines whether expanded output actually holds up.

Attention now turns to ramping volumes and proving the yields stay consistent at scale. That part isn't simple. Catalyst conditioning demands operators confirm new systems perform reliably under full production loads, and only then do long-term supply contracts become realistic. How fast that validation phase closes out will decide how quickly the added capacity turns into fuel carriers can actually buy.

For airlines facing tighter emissions rules and sharper scrutiny from passengers, a bigger domestic SAF supply carries real weight. More availability means carriers can shift from one-off spot purchases toward structured offtake agreements, the kind that make fleet decarbonization planning less of a guessing game. Scale changes the equation entirely. Producing 150 million gallons annually puts Great Falls among North America's most significant SAF hubs, handing buyers a sourcing option at a volume they simply haven't had before.

With the expansion running and validation underway, Montana Renewables looks positioned to scale through the back half of 2026. Whatever momentum builds during this stretch will likely shape the commercial commitments that follow.

text:
Coordinated National Effort to Meet International Aviation Decarbonization Standards

India has initiated a comprehensive, cross-sectoral strategy to develop a verified carbon accounting framework and establish reliable domestic supply chains for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). This initiative aims to position the country’s aviation sector for compliance with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) well ahead of the global enforcement deadline set for January 1, 2027.

Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu recently convened an inter-ministerial meeting to evaluate India’s preparedness for CORSIA implementation and the integration of SAF into the aviation fuel mix. The meeting included senior officials from the Ministries of Petroleum & Natural Gas, Environment, Forest and Climate Change, as well as representatives from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Airports Authority of India (AAI), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), and Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). The discussions focused on the progress of SAF production projects led by oil marketing companies, the development of supply chain logistics, and the necessary infrastructure to ensure consistent SAF availability.

India’s strategy targets a 5% blending of SAF by 2030, aiming to foster a robust domestic market while enhancing the country’s position as a global exporter of sustainable fuels. Minister Naidu emphasized that decarbonization represents not only an environmental necessity but also a strategic economic opportunity. He highlighted the government’s commitment to building a globally competitive SAF ecosystem that supports aviation growth and contributes to international climate goals, aligning with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of “One Earth, One Family, One Future.” The initiative is also designed to benefit multiple stakeholders, including farmers, by integrating agricultural residues into the SAF supply chain.

Progress and Challenges in Scaling Sustainable Aviation Fuel

Significant strides have been made in greening India’s aviation infrastructure, with 104 airports now operating entirely on green energy, a remarkable increase from zero in 2014. Efforts to modernize the aircraft leasing ecosystem are facilitating the operation of more fuel-efficient fleets by domestic airlines. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scaling up SAF production to meet blending targets, ensuring cost competitiveness relative to conventional jet fuels, and developing resilient supply chains for raw materials such as crop residues.

Market analysts anticipate that India’s push for SAF will stimulate increased investment in related infrastructure and technology. This momentum may also prompt other countries to accelerate their own SAF production efforts to maintain competitiveness and secure market share in the evolving global aviation fuel market.

Minister Naidu called on industry leaders to transition swiftly from feasibility assessments to definitive production schedules. He stressed the importance of clear obligations for all stakeholders concerning production capacity and carbon accounting. India’s immediate priority is to meet the 1% SAF blending mandate under CORSIA in a cost-effective manner, while simultaneously developing a carbon-credit offset mechanism through a coordinated government approach to ensure long-term sustainability.

Policy Development and Inter-Ministerial Coordination

The Minister underscored the necessity of collective decision-making and seamless coordination among ministries to drive the energy transition forward. The meeting reviewed progress on SAF supply chain development, the establishment of a national SAF Registry, and compliance measures for CORSIA. Minister Naidu expressed confidence in the commitment of government bodies and industry participants, directing all stakeholders to expedite key deliverables to guarantee India’s full operational readiness before the mandatory phase of CORSIA begins.

He also confirmed that the draft SAF policy is nearing completion, following extensive inter-ministerial consultations and stakeholder engagement. Throughout the policy development process, minimizing financial burdens on air travelers and airlines has remained a central priority, reflecting India’s balanced approach to advancing its sustainable aviation agenda.

description:

The details: X1 spans 106 feet, measures 76 feet nose to tail, and weighed more than 25,000 pounds at takeoff.
The company targets more than 40% lower operating costs than legacy regional aircraft, citing cheaper energy, simpler maintenance, and greater uptime.

text:
What's the deal? Heart Aerospace has completed the first flight of its X1 demonstrator, which it says is the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown. The 27-minute piloted flight took place on August 12 at Plattsburgh International Airport in upstate New York, where the aircraft taxied, took off, climbed, manoeuvred and landed.

The details: X1 spans 106 feet, measures 76 feet nose to tail, and weighed more than 25,000 pounds at takeoff. It reached 1,100 feet and its all-electric propulsion delivered over one megawatt of power, using roughly $5 of electricity.

Why it matters: Heart framed that $5 against surging fuel costs. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 per gallon in the week ending August 7, up 63% year over year — highlighting the case for shielding airlines from oil-market volatility.

What's the endgame? X1 is a demonstrator for the ES-30, a fixed-wing, 30-seat regional airliner targeting service in 2031. Notably, the ES-30 is hybrid-electric, not electric: it carries a combustion range extender, giving about 200km on batteries alone and roughly 800km with the extender running.

The numbers: Heart holds $9.4bn in customer commitments from United Airlines, Air Canada, and JSX. The company targets more than 40% lower operating costs than legacy regional aircraft, citing cheaper energy, simpler maintenance, and greater uptime.

What the backers say: "Electric commercial aircraft have real potential to deliver a better travel experience for passengers while strengthening our business," said Michael Leskinen, chief financial officer of United Airlines. Air Canada's John Di Bert called the ES-30 part of a broader energy transition alongside efficiencies and sustainable aviation fuel.

What could go wrong? A commitment is not a firm order, and orders convert to revenue only after certification. The $5 figure covers energy for one flight, not maintenance, crew, airport fees, or the aircraft itself — where regional aviation economics actually sit.

Why now? The milestone follows delays and a relocation. X1 was unveiled in Sweden in September 2024 with flight testing planned for the second quarter of 2025; Heart then closed its Gothenburg operation and moved the aircraft and headquarters to the US.

The signal: Part of Heart's business case is regulatory, assuming emissions charges keep rising. The ES-30 will also fly with a single pilot at first, with autonomy envisaged later — a harder sell for passengers than the batteries. For now, the largest electric aircraft ever flown is a test article for a plane that will still burn fuel, an honest measure of where battery energy density stands.

Rolls-Royce has options abroad, Airbus and Boeing have their own timetable, and the next opening may not come for a generation.
text:
Rolls-Royce has put Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new government on notice. Chief Executive Tufan Erginbilgic says Britain must decide soon whether to co-invest in a next-generation engine for short-haul jets, or the company may place the work in another country.

The 40,000 figure refers to jobs the program could create across Rolls-Royce and its supply chain, not existing positions already marked for cuts.

The fight is about more than factories and paychecks. The proposed UltraFan 30 engine is being developed for the next generation of single-aisle aircraft, with Rolls-Royce targeting up to 20% lower fuel use than engines operating today and compatibility with 100% sustainable aviation fuel.

Since single-aisle jets are expected to dominate aircraft deliveries for the next two decades, a decision made now could shape emissions, technology, and supply chains well into the 2040s.

A deadline set by Airbus and Boeing

Erginbilgic told reporters at the Farnborough International Airshow that Airbus and Boeing could make engine decisions for their next aircraft within two years. Rolls-Royce therefore needs clarity on British support quickly enough to complete development, secure a manufacturing partner, and make a credible offer to either airplane maker.

“We would like to do it in the U.K. because of our origin. Do we have other options? Yes,” he said. The company is also talking with other governments, while Germany and the United States have been linked to possible alternatives.

The timing became more complicated after Keir Starmer stepped down and Burnham entered Downing Street. Talks had been progressing before the leadership change, although Erginbilgic said he was encouraged by the appointment of John Healey as chancellor because of Healey’s previous defense brief and familiarity with Rolls-Royce.

Still, no complete project-specific funding deal has been announced.

The money is not a blank check

Calling this a $4 billion engine project is useful shorthand, but it does not tell the whole story. In February, Erginbilgic told investors that Rolls-Royce’s spending could range from roughly $4 billion to $8 billion over 12 years, depending on the partnership, the common engine core, and the number of versions requested by aircraft manufacturers.

He also stressed that Rolls-Royce was “not asking for any loan.” The company wants research and development co-funding of the kind it says competitors receive, rather than a rescue package for a weak balance sheet. That distinction matters.

Rolls-Royce reported about $4.7 billion in underlying operating profit for 2025 and announced roughly $9.4 billion to $12 billion in share buybacks through 2028. That financial strength is likely to make any taxpayer contribution politically sensitive, even as the company argues that rival engine programs receive two or three times as much public research support.

Britain has already offered partial support

Burnham’s government announced an aerospace package worth about $803 million one day after the CEO’s comments. More than $669 million was allocated to aerospace research and technology, while about $134 million was proposed for a supply chain fund involving companies including Rolls-Royce, Airbus, Safran, and GKN Aerospace.

The government specifically said the research portfolio includes Rolls-Royce projects that build on UltraFan and prepare the company for the narrowbody market. However, the announcement did not publicly identify how much money would go to this engine, nor did it confirm support through certification and full industrialization.

In practical terms, Britain has shown that it wants to help. What Rolls-Royce is still seeking appears to be a clear, long-term commitment large enough to keep the main development and production footprint in the country.

Why UltraFan matters for emissions

UltraFan 30 is a ducted, geared turbofan planned for ground testing in 2028. Its gearbox allows the turbine and the fan to run at more efficient speeds, while carbon-titanium fan blades, a composite casing, advanced materials, and additive manufacturing are intended to reduce fuel use, emissions, weight, and production waste.

For airlines, burning less fuel means lower operating costs. For the climate, it generally means less carbon dioxide from each trip when conventional jet fuel is used. But this is not a zero-emission engine, and compatibility with sustainable aviation fuel does not guarantee that enough genuinely low-carbon fuel will be available at an affordable price.

That caveat is important because air travel keeps growing. The International Energy Agency estimated that aviation emissions rose about 5.5% in 2024, while Airbus now forecasts 3.9% annual passenger traffic growth through 2045. Efficiency is essential, but demand can swallow the gains.

The largest aircraft market is at stake

Airbus expects the world to need 42,060 new aircraft by 2045, with 81% of them in the single-aisle category. Boeing’s latest forecast is similar, projecting 33,545 single-aisle deliveries and a global fleet of more than 36,000 such jets by 2045. This is the everyday backbone of aviation, from busy domestic routes to the short European flights familiar to millions of travelers.

Rolls-Royce has been absent from this new-engine market for about 15 years. Today, the Airbus A320neo is offered with engines from CFM International or Pratt & Whitney, while Boeing’s 737 MAX uses CFM’s LEAP-1B. Re-entering means dislodging established suppliers with factories, service networks, and decades of airline data behind them.

The technology race is moving quickly too. CFM’s RISE program is targeting more than 20% better fuel efficiency for a future engine expected in the second half of the 2030s. A clever demonstrator is only the ticket to the race.

What Britain must decide

The unresolved question is not simply whether public money should be used. It is what Britain would receive in return, including domestic research, manufacturing, apprenticeships, export income, environmental milestones, and protections if production later moves abroad. A carefully structured agreement could share risk without writing a blank check.

There is also a strategic angle beyond passenger jets. Rolls-Royce says the same national skills pipeline supports advanced civil aerospace and defense work, including the Global Combat Air Programme. Losing the narrowbody opportunity could therefore weaken a wider engineering base that takes years to rebuild.

For Burnham’s government, the runway is short. Rolls-Royce has options abroad, Airbus and Boeing have their own timetable, and the next opening may not come for a generation.

title: Europe built the world's largest electric plane. It flew in New York - TNW
description:
So the world’s largest electric aircraft is a test article for a plane that will still burn fuel.
United’s chief financial officer Michael Leskinen said electric aircraft have “real potential to deliver a better travel experience for passengers”.
Heart calls itself a Los Angeles-based electric aircraft manufacturer in its press material.
Where it sits against the rest of the field Electric flight has produced more announcements than aircraft.
Electric flight depends on cells getting denser and lighter, and nothing else in the programme substitutes for that.
text:
Heart Aerospace flew its X1 demonstrator at Plattsburgh International Airport on 12 August, the company announced. The aircraft taxied, took off, climbed, manoeuvred and landed.

It reached 335 metres, and its all-electric propulsion produced more than one megawatt.

The airframe explains the record. The X1 has a wingspan of about 32 metres, runs 23 metres nose to tail, and takes off at more than 11,300kg.

Plattsburgh serves a community of 20,000 people, which is the kind of place the finished aircraft is meant to fly to.

The number that will travel

The electricity for the flight cost roughly $5. Heart puts it at approximately $5, while Engadget reported the figure as less than $5.

Heart set that against the fuel it replaces. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in the week ending 7 August, up 63% year on year.

That comparison is the point of the $5. Without it the number is merely small.

Now the scepticism. That $5 is the energy cost of one demonstration flight, not the operating cost of an airline.

It excludes maintenance, crew, airport fees, battery replacement and the capital cost of the aircraft. That is where regional aviation economics actually sit.

What it illustrates is real. Fuel is one of the largest controllable costs on a short route, and it moves with oil markets and carbon pricing. Electricity makes that bill predictable, which airlines value nearly as much.

What the company is actually building

The X1 is a demonstrator. The product is the ES-30, a conventional fixed-wing airliner with 30 seats, and here is the detail most coverage buries.

The ES-30 is hybrid-electric, not electric. It carries a combustion range extender alongside its batteries.

The range figures explain why. Heart targets about 200km on batteries alone, rising to roughly 800km with the range extender running.

So the world’s largest electric aircraft is a test article for a plane that will still burn fuel. That is the honest state of battery energy density, and Heart is clear about it.

The first pre-production ES-30 is taking shape at the company’s pilot manufacturing plant in Los Angeles. Flight testing begins in 2028, certification runs under FAA Part 25, and Heart targets entry into service in 2031.

The commercial claim is a cut of more than 40% in operating costs against legacy regional aircraft. Heart itemises it as lower energy costs, cheaper maintenance from simpler electric propulsion, and better uptime from an integrated electronics and software architecture.

The company expects that gap to widen. It cites battery advances, crew-efficiency gains, and low exposure to the emissions taxes and fees spreading through aviation worldwide.

Read that last item twice. Part of the business case is regulatory, and it assumes those charges keep rising.

One pilot now, none later

The crew-efficiency line has a specific meaning. The ES-30 will fly with a single pilot at first, and Heart envisages autonomous service after that.

Engadget flagged that as the more concerning half of the plan. Passengers who have made peace with electric propulsion may take longer over an empty seat at the front.

The customers, and what a commitment is

Heart says it holds $9.4bn in customer commitments. United Airlines, Air Canada and JSX are the named customers.

A commitment is not an order, and an order is not revenue. Aviation runs on options, letters of intent and conditional purchases that convert only after certification.

The airlines are invested as well as interested. United’s chief financial officer Michael Leskinen said electric aircraft have “real potential to deliver a better travel experience for passengers”.

Air Canada’s John Di Bert framed it as a portfolio rather than a bet. The energy transition, he said, will need operational efficiencies, sustainable aviation fuel and new aircraft technologies together.

Both quotes came from finance chiefs rather than fleet planners, which is the correct register for a 2031 aircraft.

Europe designed it and America is flying it

Here is the part that should interest European tech. Heart Aerospace started in Gothenburg, and it no longer operates there.

In April 2025 it announced it was relocating to Los Angeles and closing its Swedish operations entirely.

Chief executive Anders Forslund gave the reasons plainly at the time. The move would support experimental flights of the X1 and a future X2, allow deeper vertical integration on batteries and software, and put the company nearer to customers and investors who are increasingly American.

The company’s own description has caught up with the move. Heart calls itself a Los Angeles-based electric aircraft manufacturer in its press material.

A Swedish aviation startup has stopped describing itself as European at all.

A pattern, not an incident

The demonstrator flew under an FAA Special Airworthiness Certificate in the Experimental Category, from an American airport, with American and Canadian airlines as backers.

Europe supplied the founding idea, the early engineering and the initial funding. The United States supplied the customers, the certification path and the capital.

That division of labour is the European tech complaint in a single aircraft. Europe funds the science and then reads about the product launch.

It is the same argument that runs through every debate about digital sovereignty, and an aeroplane makes it harder to wave away than a cloud contract.

The counterargument stands up. Regional aviation is a bigger market in North America, the FAA experimental route is well trodden, and a company that needs to fly prototypes goes where it can fly them.

Where it sits against the rest of the field

Electric flight has produced more announcements than aircraft. Beta Technologies has run first flights in a US pilot programme, and Boeing has sold out of eVTOL to Archer.

Others chase different physics. Destinus is building a hydrogen jet, and XPeng has taken 7,000 orders for a flying car it showed in Germany.

Engadget sets Heart alongside Boom Supersonic, Harbour Air, ZeroAvia and Rolls-Royce, a field mostly chasing air taxis, engines or speed rather than a certified airliner.

Heart is doing something harder and duller. The ES-30 targets the short hops now flown by regional aircraft such as the Embraer ERJ, under the same certification regime as a Boeing.

Chief technology officer Ben Stabler said the flight showed Heart can “design, build, test, operate, and continuously improve a clean-sheet electric commercial aircraft”. On the evidence of one 27-minute flight, the aircraft covers the first four.

What would settle it

Three things are checkable rather than promotional. The first is the X2, because a second demonstrator flying on schedule is the difference between a milestone and a programme.

The second is conversion. Watch how much of that $9.4bn turns into firm orders once certification looks credible.

The third is the battery, and Engadget makes the point bluntly. Electric flight depends on cells getting denser and lighter, and nothing else in the programme substitutes for that.

A 2031 service date is ambitious by the standards of aircraft development. Forslund calls electrification the heart of a vision for “abundant air travel”, with cleaner and more frequent service to airports closer to home.

He is probably right about the physics. Whether Europe gets any of the industrial benefit came down to an announcement in April 2025, one that drew far less attention than a 27-minute flight.

title: Europe widens its lead over US, Asia in switch to cleaner jet fuel - Luxembourg Times
description:

But with cleaner jet fuel costing two-to-three times as much as conventional fuel, voluntary demand has remained weak.

That’s why some green groups hesitate to use the phrase “sustainable aviation fuel” when describing these alternate propellants.
text:
When it comes to cleaner jet fuel, the stick is proving mightier than the carrot.

European airlines surged ahead in their use of sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, last year, while carriers in the US and Asia fell further behind, according to a Bloomberg analysis of dozens of airline environmental filings.

British Airways’ parent company IAG led passenger airlines with 3.3% of its jet fuel coming from SAF, followed by Air France-KLM at 2.9% and Ryanair at 2.0%. US airlines, meanwhile, hovered between 0.3% and 1%.

The growth has largely been driven by mandates in the EU and UK, which kicked in last year and require 2% of jet fuel to be SAF. That obligation steps up to 3.6% this year in the UK.

The US, by contrast, has shied away from SAF mandates amid opposition from airlines. Federal and state governments instead offer financial incentives to boost production. But with cleaner jet fuel costing two-to-three times as much as conventional fuel, voluntary demand has remained weak.

“The numbers show that the mandates work,” said Camille Mutrelle, aviation policy manager at Transport & Environment, a nonprofit in Brussels.

IAG alone purchased more SAF last year than all US airlines combined. The owner of British Airways, Aer Lingus and Iberia bought more than 375 million litres, compared with about 367 million litres consumed by major US carriers, according to industry group Airlines for America.

The group, however, says the market is still too immature to conclude that mandates work far better than voluntary efforts. It also points out that SAF consumption in the US more than doubled last year.

“We’ve seen an incredible amount of progress in the US despite all the challenges in the market,” said Kevin Welsh, Airlines for America’s vice president of environmental affairs.

When including logistics and delivery companies, Germany-based DHL Group leads the planet, with 10% of its jet fuel coming from SAF.

Europe’s gains mask a slower global shift. SAF consumption doubled worldwide last year, yet accounted for just 0.6% of jet fuel. The International Air Transport Association expects that to rise to 0.8% this year as growth slows.

That tepid increase could undercut the voluntary pledges of airlines, with dozens promising to reach 10% SAF by 2030. Even with SAF expected to grow sixfold by the end of the decade, it will only account for about 3.5% of the world’s jet fuel, according to estimates from Bloomberg.

Such expectations could climb, though, as more countries follow Europe’s approach. South Korea will require a 1% SAF blend for international flights departing the country starting next year, while Singapore will impose a levy on airline tickets to help fund purchases of the cleaner fuel. The Canadian province of British Columbia will introduce a 1% renewable-fuel requirement for jet fuel in 2028. Other governments, from Turkey to Indonesia, are also pursuing SAF mandates.

As SAF production ramps up, securing enough low-carbon feedstocks will be a big challenge. Much of today’s cleaner jet fuel is made from used cooking oil and animal fats, but supplies are limited. Environmentalists worry that surging demand could boost reliance on crops to produce the fuel, which could bring its own environmental costs, from fertiliser use to the clearing of forests and grasslands.

That’s why some green groups hesitate to use the phrase “sustainable aviation fuel” when describing these alternate propellants. “Sustainability has to be earned and demonstrated, not just assumed,” said Tim Johnson, director of Aviation Environment Federation, a nonprofit in the UK.

One highly anticipated solution is e-SAF, a next-generation fuel made using renewable electricity, hydrogen and captured CO2. It can cut emissions by 90%. But the technology remains in its infancy, with the fuel only available in “laboratory quantities” and costing up to ten-times more than conventional fuel, according to Lufthansa.

US startup Twelve opened one such facility in Moses Lake, Washington, in June. Even when operating at full tilt, the plant will only produce about 189,000 litres a year – roughly the amount needed to fly a 747 from New York to London and back.

Twelve plans to develop much larger US plants capable of producing tens of millions of litres annually, though it declined to disclose their potential locations or provide a more precise timeline.

With just a couple of other e-SAF plants under construction around the world, Mutrelle of Transport & Environment worries supplies will fall far short of what’s needed in the coming years.

“The situation is becoming more and more concerning,” she said.

title: How U.S. Healthcare Can Better Protect the Environment and Your Health
description:

While the federal government remains polarized on issues surrounding healthcare and the environment, a new paper argues that healthcare systems can mitigate this impact by adopting the principles of Private Environmental Governance (PEG), a model for private action that has already produced significant benefits inother industries.
“Private Health Governance and the Environment,” by Lauren R. Roth and Ethan Thorpe, calls for hospitals and accreditors to adopt what they call Private Health Governance standards to promote energy efficiency while reducing waste and emissions.
Because environmental and human health are intertwined, “applying PEG tactics to healthcare is not just a practical, but a necessary step forward for the U.S. healthcare system,” they write.
“Private Health Governance” analyzes the history of PEG, how private organizations have adopted its tactics, and where it could help in the healthcare sector.
text:
The U.S. healthcare system produces roughly 8.5% of the country’s total carbon emissions. While the federal government remains polarized on issues surrounding healthcare and the environment, a new paper argues that healthcare systems can mitigate this impact by adopting the principles of Private Environmental Governance (PEG), a model for private action that has already produced significant benefits inother industries.

“Private Health Governance and the Environment,” by Lauren R. Roth and Ethan Thorpe, calls for hospitals and accreditors to adopt what they call Private Health Governance standards to promote energy efficiency while reducing waste and emissions. They argue that efforts like Walmart’s Project Gigaton, which eliminated more than 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide from its operations in less than seven years, prove PEG’s ability to reduce environmental degradation, even if they are not solutions unto themselves.

Because environmental and human health are intertwined, “applying PEG tactics to healthcare is not just a practical, but a necessary step forward for the U.S. healthcare system,” they write.

“Private Health Governance” analyzes the history of PEG, how private organizations have adopted its tactics, and where it could help in the healthcare sector. They also discuss the value of promoting PEG’s economic benefits and maintaining a connection between environmental and health law in the wake of the EPA’s decision to stop considering lives saved when setting rules on air pollution.

“Isolating environmental and health law at a time when both face unprecedented retrenchment is a tactic that can be combatted with efforts to promote synergies between the two fields,” the authors note.

The Economic Benefits of Private Health Governance

While the article concedes that PEG initiatives would involve significant up-front investment for healthcare providers, it denotes many tactics that provide significant savings at little to no cost. Managing usage of energy-intensive imaging technology like MRIs, automated medication dispensing systems, and transitioning from inhaled to intravenous anesthetics quickly reduce energy consumption and expenditures.

For larger, capital-intensive efforts, “green” financing opportunities can help offset the expense, allowing systems to undertake resilience projects that save assets in the event of extreme weather events.

How to Implement Private Health Governance

The authors recommend any PHG initiative start “with the most apparent changes.” They point to airlines, which have been slow to adopt costly sustainable aviation fuel but more willing to eliminate single-use plastics on flights. “Simple methods like this,” they note, “can help organizations fill gaps between environmental needs and current practices.”

Likewise, they advocate for setting standards that include carrots as well as sticks, with flexibility to account for the realities of healthcare providers operating in different environments. Large organizations can lend resources to help partners meet their own goals; they cite Walmart’s partnership with HSBC to offer better financing terms for suppliers engaging in sustainability projects as a prominent example.

A Stopgap That Addresses Environmental and Health Challenges

The article confronts stark realities about the state of healthcare in the U.S. “Excessive costs are passed on to patients who pay more in the United States than peer countries but receive inferior care. Meanwhile, overtreatment, waste, and low-value care make the U.S. healthcare system the most environmentally damaging in the world.”

At a time when “public governance is unlikely to address the underlying problems,” the authors propose using private alternatives “as a gap-filling measure.”

“Embedding environmental sustainability into accreditation, which is already overwhelmingly performed by private organizations, can induce life-saving and cost-effective changes throughout the healthcare system while promoting every pillar of healthcare quality.”

title: NCGA Urges Revised Codes to Measure the Growing Bioeconomy

text:
Domestic biodiesel consumption was forecast to increase by 1% in 2026 compared to the previous year to 350M litres, the 23 July ‘Philippines – Biofuels Annual’ said.

Biodiesel production was expected to reach 370M litres in 2026, up 6% from the revised 2025 production level.

“This growth is supported by rising consumption under the current B3 mandate, and the increase in the number of biodiesel producers from 13 in 2025 to 15 this year,” the USDA said.

According to industry sources, existing biodiesel plants could support blends up to B7, suggesting that current production infrastructure could cope with B5 implementation.

“Industry contacts also note that while the bulk of coconut oil continues to flow to traditional export markets, the local biodiesel industry offers coconut farmers a more predictable market, an advantage that would become more pronounced with the implementation of higher blend mandates,” the USDA said.

In the Philippines, biodiesel is currently produced from coconut oil transesterified into coco methyl ester (CME), according to the report.

Increasing the biodiesel blending mandate would require sustained development of domestic feedstock sources to ensure adequate supply, the USDA said.

Meanwhile, although the Philippines currently has no domestic sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production, efforts to develop the sector gained further traction in 2026, according to the report.

A multi-stakeholder working group was set up to accelerate priority actions for developing the country’s SAF industry and several partnerships were also forged, including developing SAF from coconut-based feedstocks, and creating a platform for capacity building and knowledge exchange.

The Philippine government had also highlighted SAF as a measure under its fuel transition plan for the transport sector, although details of the plan had not been released at the time of the report.

In addition, a study to assess the feasibility of local SAF production was being conducted by the Department of Transport, the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) and global aircraft manufacturer Airbus. The study would cover macro-economic data analysis, SAF feedstocks and production pathways evaluation, financing assessment and policy support, and an action plan, the report said.

“The study will support policy development and is expected to encourage industry stakeholders to advance SAF production in the Philippines,” the USDA said.
