text:
The country had achieved a notable milestone in renewable energy, reaching its Paris Agreement non-fossil fuel capacity target years ahead of schedule and securing a leading global position, the 23 July ‘India – Biofuels Annual’ said.

However, the biodiesel programme faces considerable challenges from feedstock supply constraints that could hold back blending plans, according to the report.

Meanwhile, India was taking important steps with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for international flights and sustainable maritime fuel development, positioning itself as a regional leader in transportation fuel innovation, the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) report said.

Biodiesel blending in India was expected to remain below 1% in 2026, well below the 5% target for 2030.

Feedstock availability represented the main constraint on further expansion, the report said.

India’s biodiesel production relies on diverse feedstocks, including animal fats, non-edible oils, used cooking oil (UCO), and imported palm oil and palm stearin.

Although used cooking oil (UCO) consumption was at a record high, collection remained logistically difficult and UCO availability was projected to increase only marginally due to a decline in edible oil availability.

India’s domestic edible oil production was expected to decrease in 2026, with imports also expected to decline due to geopolitical instability in West Asia.

Despite this, Indian biodiesel production was forecast to total 640M litres in 2026, a 15% increase compared to the 2025 revised estimate of 556M litres.

Biodiesel consumption was also projected to increase by approximately 18% in 2026 from the revised 2025 estimate of 475M litres to 560M litres.

Additionally, palm stearin consumption was trending up in 2026 but remained below historical levels due to reduced Indonesian exports.

Overall, installed biodiesel capacity totalled 2bn litres, with usage of around one-third due to feedstock limitations.

Indian exports of biodiesel imports in 2025 were negligible, and this trend was expected to continue throughout the current year.

Exports were forecast to increase in 2026 from 76M litres the previous year to 110M litres due to increased demand from the European Union (EU), as it looked to offset lower biodiesel imports from Argentina.

India was also advancing SAF development with mandatory blending targets of 1% for international flights by 2027, moving to 5% by 2030. Indian Oil Corporation (IOCL) received India's first international certification in December 2025 and currently produced 30,000 tonnes/year of SAF.

As one of the largest consumers of edible oils globally, India held a strategic advantage for hydrotreated esters and fatty acids (HEFA)-based SAF production from UCO, the report said.

However, the supply chain presented difficulties, particularly in collecting UCO from both industrial facilities and residential households, which could hold the sector back, the USDA said.

Sustainable maritime fuel development was also progressing, with a major Indian port achieving a standard that could support 500,000 tonnes of methanol availability by 2028/29.

title: EU approves $335 million Dutch schemes to boost sustainable aviation fuel production
description:
The European Commission has approved two Dutch schemes worth a combined $335 million to support sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production and the development of new SAF projects as the European Union seeks to expand supplies of lower-carbon aviation fuels.
One of the schemes will provide investment aid for SAF production facilities, while the other will fund preparatory activities for projects.
These include advanced bio-SAF produced through pathways other than the widely used Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) process, as well as synthetic aviation fuel, or e-SAF.
Projects receiving production support will have to meet EU sustainability requirements applicable to renewable fuels of non-biological origin and advanced biofuels.
The Commission said the schemes would help strengthen SAF production capacity while supporting Europe’s broader efforts to reduce emissions from aviation and develop a competitive low-carbon industrial sector.
text:
The European Commission has approved two Dutch schemes worth a combined $335 million to support sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production and the development of new SAF projects as the European Union seeks to expand supplies of lower-carbon aviation fuels.

The schemes, approved under EU State aid rules, will provide funding for SAF production facilities as well as early-stage project development, including front-end engineering design studies, ESG News reported.

The Commission said the measures are aligned with the EU’s Clean Industrial Deal and will support the implementation of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, which aims to increase the use of SAF in the aviation sector.

Projects receiving support are expected to produce around 285 kilotonnes of SAF annually, equivalent to about 350 million litres of kerosene or the fuel required for roughly 3,500 intercontinental flights.

One of the schemes will provide investment aid for SAF production facilities, while the other will fund preparatory activities for projects. Both will draw from the same overall funding allocation.

The aid will be provided as direct grants after beneficiaries meet specified project milestones. Applications will be assessed on a first-come-first-served basis, with the Commission requiring the process to be objective, transparent and non-discriminatory.

The schemes will operate from 2027 until 2031 at the latest, with up to five funding rounds possible depending on the availability of funds.

The Netherlands is targeting two SAF technologies that are at an earlier stage of commercial development. These include advanced bio-SAF produced through pathways other than the widely used Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) process, as well as synthetic aviation fuel, or e-SAF.

Dutch authorities expect early public support to help these technologies move towards commercialisation while maintaining technological diversity as demand for SAF grows across Europe.

Projects receiving production support will have to meet EU sustainability requirements applicable to renewable fuels of non-biological origin and advanced biofuels.

The Commission said the schemes would help strengthen SAF production capacity while supporting Europe’s broader efforts to reduce emissions from aviation and develop a competitive low-carbon industrial sector.

The Corporation benefited from higher realized margins on these volumes and the recognition of the BPI.

Canadian regulatory developments

As previously disclosed in the Corporation's MD&A for the year ended December 31, 2025, and the three months ended March 31, 2026, Tidewater Renewables formally submitted its application for the BPI in January 2026 and received conditional approval on March 30, 2026.

The Corporation is pleased to report that subsequent to the quarter-end, on July 7, 2026, Tidewater Renewables successfully executed the Contribution Agreement. With this final milestone achieved, total available funds under the program are confirmed to be in line with HDRD Complex's total annual production capacity.

Management anticipates receiving both the first and second quarter program payments in the third quarter of 2026, with subsequent BPI contributions expected to be received quarterly in arrears, providing a consistent and meaningful boost to the HDRD Complex's economics, liquidity, and overall profitability throughout the duration of the program's incentive window.

Hedging program

To further protect the Corporation's financial position, management has continued its proactive hedging program. As previously disclosed, the Corporation has approximately 50% renewable diesel (and attached emission credit) sales and associated feedstock purchases hedged for the balance of 2026.

Looking ahead to 2027, subsequent to June 30, 2026, the Corporation has extended this strategy by securing further hedges for approximately 20% of anticipated 2027 renewable diesel (and attached emission credit) sales and associated feedstock purchases, at significantly improved fixed prices relative to the 2026 hedges. By utilizing these derivative instruments, the Corporation has locked in gross margin on a portion of production, effectively reducing exposure to commodity pricing volatility and ensuring more predictable cash flows.

SAF development update

Tidewater Renewables continues to advance its proposed 6,500 bbl/d SAF project in British Columbia. Optimization work on the project has now been completed, which was partially funded by the emission credits received under the previously disclosed September 2025 amended initiative agreement.

On June 19, 2026, the Corporation executed a New Initiative Agreement with the Government of British Columbia, providing for additional BC LCFS Credits. These new BC LCFS credits are intended to support advancing critical pre-FID activities of the proposed facility and mitigate execution risk. Consequently, the pre-FID activities are expected to represent the main focus of Tidewater Renewables' growth capital expenditures for the remainder of 2026, helping the Corporation advance toward a potential FID, currently targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. These pre-FID activities are expected to allow Tidewater Renewables to preserve project schedule certainty, maintain vendor and fabrication capacity availability, mature engineering deliverables, support regulatory advancement and position the project for efficient execution following the potential FID approval. The Corporation expects to receive emission credits in connection with completing the first of two milestones outlined in the New Initiative Agreement in the third quarter of 2026, with the remaining credits expected to be received in the fourth quarter of 2026.

While Tidewater Renewables remains optimistic about the SAF project's potential, the decision to proceed with the SAF project remains contingent upon the execution of long-term offtake agreements, and provincial and federal government regulatory support to facilitate obtaining committed financing.

2026 guidance update

During the second quarter of 2026, the Corporation continued to navigate the market dynamics resulting from ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The persistent volatility and elevated renewable diesel benchmarks have sustained an extremely constructive margin environment for the HDRD Complex, as realized pricing continued to outpace feedstock input costs. Additionally, as previously disclosed, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency finalized the Renewable Volume Obligations regulatory framework on March 27, 2026. This framework underpinned the intrinsic value of D4 RINs and broader market tightness during the second quarter, reinforcing the U.S. import parity benchmark pricing utilized in a significant portion of Tidewater Renewables' offtake agreements.

Reflecting these favourable market conditions combined with the Corporation's strong operational execution, Tidewater Renewables is updating its full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA(1) guidance to $130.0 million to $140.0 million (from $100.0 million to $110.0 million). All other operational metrics, including sales volumes and 2026 capital expenditure targets, remain unchanged as the Corporation continues to prioritize debt reduction and operational optimization.

HDRD Complex

The HDRD Complex is Canada's first standalone renewable diesel facility and is located adjacent to Tidewater Midstream and Infrastructure Ltd.'s PGR. The HDRD Complex is designed to process 3,000 bbl/d of renewable feedstock and utilizes renewable hydrogen to reduce the CI of the renewable fuel it produces.

During the second quarter of 2026, the HDRD Complex achieved an average utilization rate of 3,315 bbl/d, or 111% of design capacity. This compares to 2,164 bbl/d, or 72% of design capacity, during the same period in the prior year. The higher throughput reflects robust facility reliability and targeted facility debottlenecking initiatives, which collectively enabled the HDRD Complex to consistently operate above nameplate capacity. Utilization in the prior year comparative period was adversely impacted by a minor fire incident on April 1, 2025, severe weather related rail logistics challenges and softer Canadian renewable diesel demand.

text:
Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS Formula One Team is turning sustainability into a measurable performance strategy, according to Alice Ashpitel, the team’s Head of Sustainability.

The team’s recent sustainability report, carbon removals approach and supply chain work show how a racing outfit can cut emissions without dulling the spectacle.

Emissions finally turn

Alice says the most significant milestone in the report is that absolute emissions have started to fall for the first time.

“It’s the first year that absolute emissions are on that downtick,” she explains.

Formula One is a growing sport with a global calendar, and Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS F1 Team has expanded across more races and more staff. Even so, the team has begun to reverse its footprint.

“We wanted to start bringing our footprint down as quickly as possible,” Alice says.

The reduction is backed by action across race operations, including fuels, logistics and people movement. The team has also started engaging its supply chain more deeply, which Alice says is essential to making emissions cuts stick.

Turning plans into numbers

A central feature of the report is the Carbon Transition Action Plan, or CTAP, which sets out how Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS F1 Team expects to reduce emissions over time. Alice says the value of the plan lies in moving from ambition to proof.

“This is the measurable way in which we will reduce our footprint,” she says.

The plan assigns likely sources of reductions and links them to data, making the pathway easier to understand for a professional audience that wants specifics, not slogans.

Alice says that transparency is important beyond Formula One. She wants the team’s roadmap to help other travelling sports and entertainment businesses see that growth and decarbonisation can happen together.

Performance without compromise

Sustainability in Formula One cannot come at the expense of speed. For Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, the challenge is to make greener choices that still meet the extreme technical demands of racing.

“At the heart of it, sustainability and performance have to be coupled,” Alice says.

One example is the use of a bio-based carbon-fibre composite on the rear wheel shield.

Carbon fibre is a light, strong material used widely in motorsport and aerospace; in this case, the bio-based version delivered the same performance.

“It didn’t impact performance at all,” Alice says.

The part also played its role on track, helping the car to finish on the podium and then complete a further 7,000km. For Alice, that is the point: sustainability has to work in the real world, not just in a strategy document.

Formula One as test bed

Alice describes Formula One as “the world’s fastest laboratory” and the report leans heavily on that idea. The sport’s rapid development cycle allows the team to test materials, fuels and processes that may later have value well beyond racing.

She points to “brainprint” as a way of describing that wider influence. The term captures how innovations trialled in Formula One can help shape other sectors, from road transport to aerospace.

The team’s work on carbon fibre is one part of that. Its logistics trials are another. Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS F1 Team has used the first electric truck across Europe, showing that cleaner freight movement can work in a demanding international sport.

Alice says this is about proving a pathway for other industries. “If we can use it in Formula One, there are so many industries that can benefit from it,” she says.

Fuel, flight and supply chain

A second major theme in the report is travel, which remains central to Formula One’s footprint.

Mercedes-Benz AMG PETRONAS F1 Team has quadrupled its use of sustainable aviation fuel since 2022, with the intention to reduce emissions from flying, one of the sport’s hardest-to-abate areas.

The team now covers a significant share of aviation emissions with sustainable aviation fuel and has helped develop buying standards that it shares across the sport.

text:
FatHopes Energy, a Malaysian waste-based feedstock solutions for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) firm, has entered into a strategic partnership with PetroVietnam Oil Corporation (PVOIL) to establish Vietnam’s first nationwide used cooking oil (UCO) collection ecosystem for sustainable aviation fuel production.

FatHopes said in a statement on Thursday that the partnership lays the foundation for a new circular economy that transforms used cooking oil from households, restaurants, industrial kitchens, seafood processing plants and similar sources into certified renewable feedstock for SAF and other advanced biofuels.

By combining advanced digital technology, nationwide infrastructure and international sustainability standards, the collaboration is expected to accelerate Vietnam’s transition towards cleaner energy while strengthening the country’s role in the emerging global bioeconomy.

The partnership brings together FatHopes Energy’s proven expertise in UCO collection operations, digital traceability technologies and global feedstock supply chain development with PVOIL’s nationwide operational network, comprising approximately 1,000 petrol stations supported by logistics, transportation and warehousing infrastructure.

Together, the two organizations will establish a fully integrated ecosystem capable of collecting, tracing and managing UCO across Vietnam.

The initiative will commence with an initial rollout in Ho Chi Minh City before expanding progressively across the country, creating a scalable national model that supports circular economy practices, strengthens environmental governance and supplies high-quality, traceable feedstock for SAF production.

The core of the initiative is FatHopes Energy’s proprietary Waste Recycling Management System (WRMS), an advanced digital platform that provides end-to-end traceability throughout the collection journey.

Every drop of UCO collected can be digitally verified from its point of origin, ensuring compliance with international sustainability requirements while providing transparency for environmental, social and governance (ESG) reporting and global certification standards.

Beyond technology, FatHopes Energy will transfer its operational expertise, collection methodologies and international best practices developed across Southeast Asia, enabling PVOIL to rapidly build a robust and efficient nationwide collection ecosystem that meets the growing demand for sustainable feedstocks.

Leveraging their trusted national presence and operational capabilities, PVOIL and its dedicated collection subsidiary, PVOIL Trans, will lead the implementation and expansion of the initiative throughout Vietnam, engaging businesses, communities and local stakeholders to establish one of the country’s most comprehensive waste-to-energy collection networks.

The partnership also strengthens regional cooperation between Malaysia and Vietnam in advancing SAF development.

As global demand for SAF continues to accelerate, Vietnam has the opportunity to become an important contributor to the regional supply of sustainable feedstocks, while supporting its national decarbonization ambitions and broader energy transition goals.

This partnership will facilitate the aggregation of more than 200,000 tons of feedstock annually in Vietnam for export to FatHopes Energy, further strengthening its extensive feedstock portfolio.

The partnership will support FatHopes Energy’s upcoming refinery, which is positioned to serve as a regional hub for processing waste feedstocks into SAF, providing the region with a plug-and-play solution to accelerate the decarbonization of aviation.

“This partnership represents far more than the launch of a Used Cooking Oil collection program. It marks the beginning of a new circular economy for Vietnam; one where everyday waste becomes a valuable resource that contributes to cleaner skies and a more sustainable future,

“By combining FatHopes Energy’s expertise in digital traceability, feedstock collection and Sustainable Aviation Fuel supply chains with PVOIL’s nationwide reach and operational capabilities, we are building the infrastructure needed to support Vietnam’s energy transition while strengthening Southeast Asia’s role in the global sustainable aviation ecosystem,” said Vinesh Sinha, Chief Executive Officer of FatHopes Energy.

He said the firms believe this partnership will serve as a blueprint for how countries across the region can unlock the value of waste, accelerate decarbonization and create long-term environmental and economic impact.

Mai Trung Thanh, Director of PVOIL Trans, PVOIL’s dedicated collection subsidiary, said the partnership with FatHopes Energy reflects the commitment of PVOIL and PVOIL Trans to supporting Vietnam’s transition towards a more circular and sustainable economy.

“By leveraging our nationwide network together with FatHopes Energy’s innovative technology and international expertise, we are creating a modern and transparent collection ecosystem that not only delivers environmental benefits but also contributes to the future development of sustainable aviation fuel in Vietnam,” he added.

text:
Market Definition

The sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market encompasses sustainable and low-carbon aviation fuels developed, produced, blended, distributed, and utilized as alternatives to conventional fossil-based jet fuel across commercial, military, business, and unmanned aviation platforms. These fuels are designed to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while supporting long-term aviation decarbonization, energy diversification, and regulatory sustainability targets. SAF solutions include bio-based fuels, synthetic e-fuels, and emerging hydrogen-based aviation fuels compatible with evolving aircraft propulsion technologies and airport fueling ecosystems.

Modern sustainable aviation fuel solutions are developed using multiple advanced feedstocks, conversion pathways, and fuel production technologies such as hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), Fischer-Tropsch (FT), alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), catalytic hydrothermolysis jet (CHJ), co-processing, and synthetic power-to-liquid (PtL) e-fuel systems. These fuels are produced from feedstocks including used cooking oil (UCO), agricultural residues, municipal solid waste (MSW), forestry residues, algae, ethanol-based sources, renewable electricity, and captured carbon dioxide (CO2). SAF deployment varies significantly based on fuel certification limits, blending capacities, feedstock availability, production economics, refinery infrastructure, regulatory incentives, and airline sustainability commitments.

As the aviation industry globally transitions toward net-zero emission targets and energy-resilient aviation ecosystems, sustainable aviation fuel is increasingly becoming a critical pillar of aviation decarbonization strategies. These fuels enable airlines, military operators, governments, and aviation stakeholders to reduce carbon emissions without requiring immediate replacement of existing aircraft fleets, while supporting long-term environmental compliance, fuel security, and sustainable aviation operations across both developed and emerging economies.

title: Many biofuels haven't panned out. Could algae make the clean diesel and aviation fuel ...
description:
As the energy shocks of the Iran war ripple out, Australia’s leaders have scrambled to shore up supplies of fuel – especially diesel and aviation fuel.
Making biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel from these fast growing organisms can be done with much less land than other crops.
Brazil produces 22% of its own transport fuel from biofuels, while biofuels account for 6% of the fuel used in the United States.
Mandates to increase output of sustainable aviation fuel are emerging in the European Union.
Plus, it depends very heavily on imported diesel and aviation fuel.
text:
As the energy shocks of the Iran war ripple out, Australia’s leaders have scrambled to shore up supplies of fuel – especially diesel and aviation fuel.

Disruptions to fuel supplies have happened before, such as in 2008 and 2022. This disruption won’t be the last.

What should policymakers do? One option is to ramp up local production of biofuels made not from crude oil but from natural oils such as canola, animal fats – or algae.

As algae researchers, we believe these humble organisms are worth exploring. Making biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel from these fast growing organisms can be done with much less land than other crops. Technological advances mean the fuel could scale up.

Many biofuels come with trade-offs

Biofuels have gained traction worldwide as efforts to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and meet climate targets accelerate.

The Australian biofuel sector is relatively small. Farmers exported about 6 million tonnes of canola in 2023–24 to be turned into biofuels overseas.

The Australian government last year announced A$1.1 billion in incentives to boost low-carbon fuels such as biofuels.

Biofuels from corn, soybean, canola and palm oil have boosted fuel security in some nations. Brazil produces 22% of its own transport fuel from biofuels, while biofuels account for 6% of the fuel used in the United States.

The problem is, biofuels often come at an environmental cost. A third of all US corn is used to make ethanol for fuel.

What’s so good about algae?

The type we’re interested in are microalgae, single-celled organisms, not macroalgae such as kelp and other types of seaweed.

These small organisms can grow exceptionally rapidly and hold high concentrations of oils. Many microalgae species can double their weight every day. Nannochloropsis and Chlorella are the two main types used to make oil.

Traditionally, algae was grown in large, shallow outdoor pools called “raceways”. They’re now increasingly grown in high-efficiency algae bioreactors.

Algae can be processed using proven technologies such as hydrothermal liquefaction to produce biodiesel able to be used in existing trucks and machinery. It can also produce sustainable aviation fuel.

Compared to crop-based biofuels, algae has several advantages. It doesn’t compete with food production and it can be grown on non-arable land or in industrial facilities. Some species can grow in saltwater or even treat wastewater while using it for growth. If algal facilities are located near heavy industry, carbon emissions can be captured and used for algal growth in a form of carbon storage.

Algal fuels needs much less land than conventional biofuels. A hectare of algae can yield more than 58,000 litres of oil per year. By contrast, a hectare of corn produces just 172 litres.

What are the barriers?

Interest in algal fuel dates back many decades. Oil shocks in the 1970s and 1990s drove significant research into algae-based fuels. But when oil prices fell, algal biofuels were no longer cost-competitive.

Since the 1990s, technologies have matured and policy settings become more favourable. Efforts to reduce fossil fuel use have put an implicit or explicit price on carbon. Mandates to increase output of sustainable aviation fuel are emerging in the European Union.

Fossil fuel price shocks in 2022 and 2026 have nudged authorities to seriously explore alternatives. Sovereign fuel security has become a strategic priority. Both the United Arab Emirates and the US are exploring algal fuels as a long-term strategic asset.

Algae for Australia?

Australia would be well placed to explore the potential of algal fuels. It has plenty of non-arable land, abundant sunlight and some of the world’s best algae research capabilities. Plus, it depends very heavily on imported diesel and aviation fuel.

Our research group and many others have been systematically working to overcome previous limitations of algal biofuels. We now know how to produce high-quality algal fuels and scale up production at costs low enough to challenge fuels derived from crude oil.

The first step would be to invest in pilot projects to prove the technology can work at scale under real-world conditions. Overseas, similar pilots have been set up next to industry to test the use of carbon capture, or alongside research partners.

If this is successful, the next step would be to build facilities in regional locations where fossil diesel is in demand and expensive to transport – and where algae can offer a dual benefit by treating wastewater or capturing carbon.

Over time, the versatile technology could be expanded, as algae can produce not only biodiesel but also other useful products such as edible protein for animal feed and biochar, highly porous charcoal able to soak up pollutants such as heavy metals.

Algae deserves our attention

Many previous efforts to scale up biofuels have run into problems over environmental impact or cost.

It’s important to be sceptical of claims of the next big thing. But it’s also important not to overlook the potential of humble technologies such as making fuel from algae.

As leaders look for ways to bolster fuel security, algae deserves a closer look.

title: The impact of jet fuel volatility on aviation finance | Global law firm | Norton Rose Fulbright
description:
Impact on airline profitability Increases of fuel price, and limits on supply, inevitably most immediately affect airlines.
In addition, whilst a fuel hedging strategy can assist an airline in mitigating the impact of higher fuel pricing, it does not mitigate the problem of a shortage in fuel supply.
As well as the direct impact of an increase in the price of jet fuel on an airline’s cost base, the impact of higher fuel prices on the wider economy impacts airline profitability.
This could obviously impact aircraft values in the longer term – particularly those of older aircraft.
Is there an alternative to Kerosene A jet fuel?
text:
Key points

Although the aviation industry is proving to be resilient so far in the face of jet fuel price and supply volatility, from a financier’s perspective, concerns regarding a potential future deterioration in the financial performance of airlines might impact the willingness of some financiers to finance aircraft, or lead to the attempted addition of protections in financing documentation.

Higher costs and inflation can distort future aircraft valuation forecasts and can increase the residual value risk for financiers or lessors.

Engines can generally operate on sustainable aviation fuels blended with Kerosene A jet fuel, but it is not easy to find alternative fuels, in sufficient quantities, which meet the criteria for weight, flammability, energy content and freezing point.

In normal times, an estimated 20.3 million barrels of petroleum and crude oil, or roughly 25 percent of the world maritime oil trade, pass through the Strait of Hormuz every day. Hormuz is the only maritime gateway to the Persian Gulf, from where the major oil producers Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates export most of their oil. Since the start of the conflict in the Middle East, that flow has been cut to virtually zero.

Geopolitical events, such as wars, trade sanctions and political unrest in major energy-producing regions, can drive huge volatility in global crude oil markets. As a result of the conflict, and the blockade of this narrow sea channel, the price of oil, and jet fuel, has substantially increased during this year. Concerns have also been expressed in some regions regarding short and mid-term supply.

It is to be hoped that this situation will improve following the announcement of a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran which is intended to facilitate the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz. However, uncertainty remains and it is likely to be some time before the level of pre-conflict oil transit will be restored. Furthermore, it is likely that there may be a time lag between any reduction in the price of crude oil and a reduction in the price of jet fuel, as well as improvements in supply, due to depleted reserves of jet fuel and reduced refinery capacity.

Impact on airline profitability

Increases of fuel price, and limits on supply, inevitably most immediately affect airlines. Before the conflict, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), fuel already accounted for around 20-30 percent of the cost of operation. A sudden and unexpected increase in the cost of jet fuel inevitably has a huge impact on the profitability of airlines, for some of whom margins are lean at the best of times.

Airlines have sought to offset some of these increases but the measures available to them are limited. Some are well hedged for the time being, although this varies geographically. Many EU airlines are substantially hedged for 2026 but are subject to price volatilities beyond that. By contrast, US airlines tend to benefit from cheap and plentiful local supply so do not hedge, although even they need to fuel at destination airports which may not be in the US. Fuel surcharges and operational adjustments mitigate the impact, but these can only go so far. In the end, airlines either have to avoid or absorb the additional costs, or pass them on to passengers, with the risk that higher ticket prices impact demand. In addition, whilst a fuel hedging strategy can assist an airline in mitigating the impact of higher fuel pricing, it does not mitigate the problem of a shortage in fuel supply.

As well as the direct impact of an increase in the price of jet fuel on an airline’s cost base, the impact of higher fuel prices on the wider economy impacts airline profitability. Increased fuel prices often lead to inflationary pressures. It is not just airlines, and airlines’ suppliers, which buy fuel – energy prices impact every business. Increased energy costs therefore often lead to price increases which, in turn, can lead to inflation. So, airlines not only feel the impact of increased oil prices directly, but they may also see their own suppliers seeking to increase prices in response to the rising energy costs. In addition, in order to combat inflation, central banks often raise interest rates which impacts the cost of borrowing. Due to the recent progress towards resolution of the conflict with Iran, at the time of writing, many central banks are expected to hold interest rates to their current level. However, this situation is subject to change if inflationary pressures do not ease.

Economic uncertainty can also give rise to currency fluctuations. Airlines tend to be particularly exposed to variations in the value of the US dollar given that the cost of many of their outgoings including fuel costs, maintenance costs and indeed the cost of aircraft are US dollar denominated, whereas an airline’s income will frequently be denominated in other currencies. In the immediate aftermath of the start of the conflict the US dollar gained in strength against major currencies, effectively adding to the financial pressure on many airlines.

In addition, there is also the risk that an economic slowdown leads to a reduced demand for travel, particularly business travel, as businesses try to reduce costs, and in leisure travel, driven by a reduction in disposable income. Nonetheless recent IATA projections indicate that despite the economic turbulence, passenger numbers are still set to increase when compared to 2025 levels, although overall IATA have reduced their profit forecast for airlines in 2026 by half.

Airlines which are well funded are most concerned by the long-term supply issues which could limit their flying programmes. Airlines which are less well funded are more concerned that the oil price will cause financial uncertainties even before the supply issues cause concern.

Airlines are seeking external help to reduce the impact. In some regions, airlines’ lobbying has led to governments taking action to co-ordinate the supply of fuel, alleviate unnecessary costs from both slot legislation (avoiding airlines having to operate routes just to retain their slot rights) and passenger rights (confirming that cancellations caused by fuel concerns are not compensatable), and a reduction of the burden of emission trading schemes.

The impact on aviation finance

The financial performance of airlines is critical to the whole aviation financing ecosystem, whether it is the financing, leasing or operation of aircraft, so it is inevitable that one sees consequences where issues arise which impact that financial performance.

Firstly, from a financier’s perspective, concerns regarding a potential future deterioration in the financial performance of airlines may impact the willingness of some financiers to finance aircraft at all, or may lead to the attempted addition of protections in financing documentation, such as conditions precedent to drawdown relating to market deterioration which could enable a financier to refuse to advance funds in certain circumstances. Any future withdrawal of commercial financiers from aircraft finance is likely to lead to an increase in borrowing costs as competition for financing mandates decreases, and to demand for alternative forms of financing such as the export credit supported financing of aircraft.

Higher costs and inflation can also distort future aircraft valuation forecasts and can increase the residual value risk for financiers or lessors, namely the problem caused by equipment losing value more quickly than expected by the end of the lease term. This can affect financiers’ and lessors’ appetite for particular asset types, with the preference being for aircraft which will keep their value, and which will be easier to remarket in the future if necessary. It may also affect required loan to value ratios in aircraft financing transactions thus reducing the amount which a financier is willing to lend. To some extent, the risk of value deterioration has been offset by production delays at aircraft manufacturers (also exacerbated by supply chain difficulties), meaning that demand for new aircraft has continued to outstrip supply thus far, however any continuation of inflated jet fuel prices may affect this in future.

In addition, a deterioration in an airline’s profitability could mean that it is at greater risk of defaulting on its financing and leasing transactions. As a consequence, transactions may need to be restructured in order to facilitate the ability of the airline to meet its commitments or, in the worst-case scenario, that events of default are triggered and enforcement action taken. This can lead to substantial financial losses for a lessor or financier in an environment where aircraft values are reduced and opportunities to remarket the aircraft are more limited.

Whether or not an event of default has occurred is a matter of contractual interpretation. Typically, an event of default such as a non-payment event is easier to establish than reliance on an event of default relating to a more general deterioration in performance or in the market such as a material adverse change provision. It is therefore likely that lessors and financiers will want to monitor their portfolios closely and use information covenants in lease and loan documentation to obtain any necessary information regarding financial performance and the location of aircraft and engines (which often move between aircraft in an airline’s fleet). A lessor or financier may also want to monitor an airline’s financial exposure to entities such as air traffic control authorities or maintenance providers who may be able to assert a lien over an aircraft for non-payment.

From an airline’s perspective, the current economic volatility may influence its choice of financing for any acquisition of new aircraft. In times of uncertainty airlines strive to preserve cash and reduce their own exposure to residual value risk, which may make airlines consider taking aircraft on an operating lease rather than purchasing new aircraft. This may actually increase opportunities for aircraft leasing companies in an environment where demand for new more fuel-efficient aircraft remains high and there is a shortage in supply of aircraft. Airlines may also want to explore options to increase certainty as to their financing costs such as opting for fixed interest or fixed lease rates (or entering into interest rate hedging arrangements) to reduce their exposure to fluctuating interest rates.

If the elevated cost of jet fuel continues, it may lead to airlines revisiting fleeting decisions. For instance, airlines may choose to make do with existing aircraft for longer, or defer purchases of new aircraft, unless by taking new aircraft there is a substantial saving in terms of fuel burn. Airlines might also consider a different mix of routes, and possibly different aircraft to serve those routes. Some aircraft may be grounded and stored pending an easing of tensions and a resumption of full flying programmes. This could obviously impact aircraft values in the longer term – particularly those of older aircraft.

Is there an alternative to Kerosene A jet fuel?

In times of potential crisis over oil and jet fuel supply, one might think that sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) – the demand for which to date has been driven more by regulatory pressure, and emissions and blending targets, than economic advantages – might be the answer as a strategic hedge against commodity market shocks.

Engines can generally operate on alternative fuels blended with Kerosene A jet fuel, but it is not easy to find fuels, in sufficient quantities, which meet the criteria for weight, flammability, energy content and freezing point. As a result of these factors, and SAF’s availability and cost, SAF still only accounts for a very small percentage of global jet fuel, even though the emissions attributable to SAF are considered re-absorbed and therefore are not subject to emissions trading schemes. In terms of cost, SAF remains more expensive that jet fuel, but economic shocks such as the one experienced this year may further increase the interest in SAF as a hedge against kerosene products, given the consequences for energy security.

However, for the time being the aviation industry remains very largely reliant on oil, and while that continues it will be susceptible to shocks as have been felt during this year’s crisis. If in due course SAF becomes more affordable, and more plentiful, it could help the industry ride such shocks. These are all factors which those financing the aviation industry will need to stay on top of.

It is to be hoped that the recent progress made in resolving the Iranian conflict will lead to the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz and a consequent reduction in the oil price – indeed, at the time of writing, we have already seen this reduction start to occur. However, even if this progress continues, it may be longer before this leads to a consequent reduction in the price of jet fuel and a full restoration of supply. Nonetheless the aviation industry and the finance ecosystem which supports it, is used to weathering economic storms and continues to demonstrate its resilience in the face of these issues.

This article was first published in the August/September issue of Butterworths Journal of International Banking and Financial Law

title: European Commission Proposes To Extend EU ETS To International Flights Beyond Europe ...
authors: Brook  Detterman, Brook Detterman, Timothy Pohle, Ryan L. Andrée, Amandine M. Fromont
description:
Key Takeaways The European Commission has proposed revisions to the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) with significant implications for international aviation.
Many aviation stakeholders view the proposal as challenging the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) status as the only market-based measure applicable to international aviation emissions.
EU ETS Proposal Generally On July 17, 2026, the European Commission proposed revisions to EU ETS, a cornerstone of the EU’s climate policies.
As originally adopted in 2008, EU ETS was designed to cover all international flights to and from the EEA.
As a result, the Commission did not propose to extend EU ETS to cover all flights departing the EEA for destinations beyond Europe.
text:
Key Takeaways

The European Commission has proposed revisions to the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) with significant implications for international aviation.

The proposal would expand EU ETS to apply to some flights to outside of Europe but not to commercial aviation flights to and from many major aviation markets, including the U.S., India, Brazil, China, and Japan.

Beginning in 2029, EU ETS would apply to all commercial aviation departures from airports in the European Economic Area (EEA) to airports within a 5,000 km radius of Frankfurt Airport, which includes Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and major aviation hubs in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). All private business jet operations to and from the EEA would also be included.

Many aviation stakeholders view the proposal as challenging the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) status as the only market-based measure applicable to international aviation emissions.

The Commission separately proposes to strengthen support for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) by providing increased SAF allowances and supporting a book-and-claim system.

The proposal is far from final and represents only the beginning of “tripartite” negotiations among the European Commission, Council, and Parliament. Major aviation organizations, including the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the International Air Transport Association (IATA), and Airlines for America, have expressed strong opposition.

EU ETS Proposal Generally

On July 17, 2026, the European Commission proposed revisions to EU ETS, a cornerstone of the EU’s climate policies. EU ETS is a carbon pricing scheme based on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions caps and allowances and sets a legally binding target of net-zero emissions in the EU by 2050. The Commission claims that EU ETS has generated more than €270 billion for decarbonization efforts since 2005.

Signaling a less aggressive approach intended to balance economic imperatives while maintaining the EU’s commitment to achieving GHG reduction goals, the Commission’s new proposal will slow the pace at which companies must reduce emissions. The previous model targeted a net-zero emissions goal by 2039; however, this proposal’s linear reduction factor, the rate at which pollution caps fall annually, will decrease from 4.4 percent to 3.7 percent between 2031 and 2035, then at a rate of 1.7 percent annually after 2036. In its press release, the European Commission explained these changes reflect “changing global realities” and will ease the burden on European industry as the EU continues its transition to clean energy and electrification.

Impacts on the Aviation Sector

Whether EU ETS should apply to flights beyond Europe has long been linked to the development of CORSIA. As originally adopted in 2008, EU ETS was designed to cover all international flights to and from the EEA. In 2012, however, the EU adopted its "stop the clock" decision, temporarily limiting the system's application to flights within the EEA. The EU described this change as a way to support efforts to address international aviation emissions through ICAO. ICAO subsequently developed CORSIA as the sole global market-based measure for regulating CO2 emissions from international flights. In its current form, beginning in 2028, CORSIA will require carriers to purchase and retire carbon offsets for emissions exceeding 85% of their 2019 emissions levels.

The EU ETS Directive, however, required the European Commission to assess the “environmental integrity” of CORSIA and whether ICAO had sufficiently “strengthened CORSIA” by July 1, 2026, to support the EU’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement. Under the Directive, a negative assessment would trigger an obligation for the Commission to propose legislation to extend EU ETS to include “as appropriate” flights departing the EEA to destinations beyond Europe. The European Commission found that CORSIA has not “yet” been sufficiently strengthened, indicating that the program is currently insufficient but may eventually be adequate.

As a result, the Commission did not propose to extend EU ETS to cover all flights departing the EEA for destinations beyond Europe. Instead, beginning in 2029, EU ETS would apply to flights departing from airports in the EEA to destinations within 5,000 km of Frankfurt airport (the largest airport in “the geographic centre of Europe”). Importantly, the proposal would not extend EU ETS to flights: (1) arriving from airports outside the EEA (except for airports in the UK, Switzerland, and Gibraltar) to airports in the EEA; or (2) departing to airports outside the EEA (except for airports in the UK, Switzerland, and Gibraltar), located more than 5,000 km from the geographic center of Europe. In other words, flights from the EEA to Northern Africa and most of the Middle East, including theUAE, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, would be subject to EU ETS starting in 2029. Flights to and from the United States, Brazil, China, Japan, and other countries outside the 5,000 km perimeter remain excluded.

The Commission states this approach is intended “to ensure that aviation as a whole contributes its fair share to addressing climate change in line with the objectives of the Paris Agreement” while “maintain[ing] close alignment” with CORSIA by allowing it to apply, exclusive of EU ETS, to most international flights to and from EEA airports. The proposal provides for a new assessment by the Commission of CORSIA in 2032, stating that if CORSIA proves to be an effective tool for reducing emissions – i.e., it is “ambitious, efficient and successful” – the scope of EU ETS should then be retracted to cover only flights within the EEA. This implicitly acknowledges that the Commission could also recommend expansion of EU ETS to international flights involving EEA airports if its 2032 report concludes CORSIA is not “successful.”

Separately, the new EU ETS proposal aims to strengthen support for SAF by providing increased SAF allowances and supporting a book-and-claim system. The Commission states this support will rise to €15 billion from 2029-2040 compared with the current €1.5 billion over eight years. Book-and-claim systems are rapidly emerging across clean fuel markets, as they allow physical products and their environmental attributes to be transacted as separate commodities (read more about book-and-claim systems here). Developing a book-and-claim system could help bridge near‑term demand and longer‑term infrastructure build‑out for SAF.

Aviation Sector Reactions

The international aviation community’s response so far has been generally critical of the Commission’s proposal. ICAO released a statement expressing frustration with the proposal’s displacement of CORSIA within the 5,000 km perimeter and undermining of CORSIA’s status as the only market-based measure applying to international aviation emissions. According to ICAO, EU ETS expansion would introduce the potential for double charging for CO2 emissions from international aviation and possibly damage the implementation of CORSIA.

IATA also released a statement saying it is “deeply frustrated” with the proposal’s attempt to expand EU ETS beyond Europe’s borders and recommending the EU focus on making CORSIA more successful instead. IATA did recognize, however, that increasing SAF allowances and enabling a book-and-claim system for SAF could prove very helpful. Airlines for America’s statement also opposes the Commission’s proposal.

Next Steps

The proposal is far from final. The European Commission’s proposal still needs support from the 27 member states of the EU as well as from the European Parliament before finalization, meaning months of discussion lie ahead. In addition, while the proposal does not yet expand EU ETS to worldwide flights, non-EU countries currently encompassed in the proposal’s scope will likely push back against inclusion. Negotiations beyond the European approval process may thus further delay adoption.

title: SAF Process Design: Feedstocks, Conversion Pathways, and Product Requirements
description:
Preview Sustainable aviation fuel can be produced through several approved pathways, including HEFA, FT-SPK, ATJ, pyrolysis-derived routes, and methanol-based or power-to-liquid pathways.
The final product must meet aviation fuel requirements, including jet-range composition, blending limits, and relevant ASTM certification pathways.
Summary Conclusion SAF process design is a multi-pathway engineering problem where feedstock type, process route, hydrogen demand, and product specification all matter.
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) State-of-Industry Report.
Sustainable aviation fuel: Biomass fostered future aviation.
text:
Preview

Sustainable aviation fuel can be produced through several approved pathways, including HEFA, FT-SPK, ATJ, pyrolysis-derived routes, and methanol-based or power-to-liquid pathways. The right route depends on whether the feedstock is lipid-based, sugar-based, lignocellulosic biomass, waste, alcohol, or CO2 plus hydrogen in a PtL configuration.

Designing a SAF plant means matching feedstock quality, conversion chemistry, hydrogen demand, catalyst behaviour, and product specifications into one integrated process. The final product must meet aviation fuel requirements, including jet-range composition, blending limits, and relevant ASTM certification pathways.

Overview

Main SAF routes include:

HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids), using oils, fats, greases, and algae-derived lipids. These are cleaned, hydrogenated, and refined to produce a high‑quality jet fuel. HEFA is currently the most commercially mature SAF pathway.

FT-SPK (Fischer–Tropsch Synthetic Paraffinic Kerosene), using biomass or waste-derived syngas(a mix of CO + H₂). The syngas is converted via the Fischer–Tropsch process into long-chain hydrocarbons, then upgraded to jet fuel. FT‑SPK is scalable and can use municipal waste, agricultural residues, or forestry biomass. .

ATJ (Alcohol-to-Jet), using alcohols such as ethanol or isobutanol. Uses alcohols such as ethanol or isobutanol. The alcohol is dehydrated, oligomerised, and hydrogenated to produce jet-range hydrocarbons. ATJ is attractive because ethanol supply chains are already widespread.

Pyrolysis-based SAF, using biomass to make bio-oil followed by upgrading. Uses biomass (wood, residues, waste) heated without oxygen to make bio‑oil. The bio‑oil is then upgraded through hydrotreating and cracking to produce jet fuel. This pathway leverages simple thermochemical conversion but requires significant upgrading.

MtJ or PtL (Methanol-to-Jet or Power-to-Liquids), using methanol or CO2 plus green hydrogen. Uses methanol or CO₂ + green hydrogen. CO₂ is captured, combined with renewable H₂ to make methanol, which is then converted into jet fuel. This pathway enables fully synthetic, carbon‑neutral SAF when powered by renewable electricity.

Each route has different pretreatment, reactor, hydrogen, and upgrading needs. For example, HEFA is attractive for lipid feedstocks but depends on hydrogenation and hydrocracking, while FT requires gasification, gas cleaning, syngas conditioning, and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis.

Engineering insight: SAF design is fundamentally about converting very different feedstocks into one tightly controlled product family.

Real Cases

Case 1: HEFA pathway

Reviews of SAF pathways show that HEFA uses triglyceride feedstocks such as vegetable oils, animal fats, waste greases, and algae, and converts them through hydroprocessing, isomerisation, and hydrocracking. This makes HEFA one of the most mature and commercially relevant SAF routes.

Case 2: FT from biomass and waste

A review of renewable aviation fuels showed that lignocellulosic biomass and residual wastes can be converted into SAF by gasification, syngas cleaning, conditioning, FT synthesis, and hydroprocessing. This route is technically more complex, but it offers strong flexibility in feedstock choice.

Case 3: Methanol-to-jet and power-to-liquid

A recent review of the methanol pathway described a process chain involving methanol synthesis, methanol-to-olefin conversion, oligomerisation, and hydrogenation, with special focus on feedstocks, reactor design, and process layout. This illustrates how PtL routes depend not only on renewable power and CO2, but also on carefully integrated reaction and separation systems.

Pitfalls

Common pitfalls include:

choosing a route before confirming feedstock availability,

underestimating pretreatment requirements,

ignoring hydrogen demand in upgrading steps,

failing to design for product specification and blending limits,

and assuming all “renewable” feedstocks behave similarly in the conversion unit.

Another issue is overestimating the commercial readiness of a route. Some SAF pathways are mature; others remain promising but highly capital-intensive or feedstock-constrained.

Resolutions

The best resolutions usually include:

screening feedstocks before final process selection,

matching the route to local supply chains,

designing pretreatment and upgrading together,

checking product quality against certification requirements,

and comparing pathways using techno-economic and lifecycle metrics.

Engineering insight: the right SAF process is the one that aligns feedstock, chemistry, and market access from the beginning.

CAPEX

Main CAPEX drivers include:

feedstock receiving and pretreatment,

reactors and conversion units,

hydrogen supply and upgrading systems,

gas cleaning and separation equipment,

product finishing and blending infrastructure,

and utilities and storage.

Gasification-to-FT and PtL routes usually require higher capital intensity than HEFA.

OPEX

Main OPEX drivers include:

feedstock procurement,

hydrogen use,

catalyst and sorbent replacement,

utilities and power,

pretreatment and drying energy,

and compliance testing for product quality.

For SAF, feedstock logistics and hydrogen cost are often two of the biggest drivers of operating cost.

Summary Conclusion

SAF process design is a multi-pathway engineering problem where feedstock type, process route, hydrogen demand, and product specification all matter. The most successful plants are those that align the chemistry with the feedstock reality and the certification requirements of the final fuel.

In practice, SAF success comes from designing the full chain , from feedstock handling to jet-fuel product quality , rather than focusing on a single reactor step.

The partnership lays the foundation for a new circular economy that transforms UCO from households, restaurants, industrial kitchens, seafood processing plants and similar sources into certified renewable feedstock for SAF and other advanced biofuels.

The partnership brings together FatHopes Energy’s proven expertise in UCO collection operations, digital traceability technologies and global feedstock supply chain development with PVOIL’s nationwide operational network, comprising approximately 1,000 petrol stations supported by logistics, transportation and warehousing infrastructure.

Together, the two organisations will establish a fully integrated ecosystem capable of collecting, tracing and managing UCO across Vietnam.

The initiative will commence with an initial rollout in Ho Chi Minh City before expanding progressively across the country, creating a scalable national model that supports circular economy practices, strengthens environmental governance and supplies high-quality, traceable feedstock for SAF production.

Vinesh Sinha, CEO of FatHopes Energy, said: “This partnership represents far more than the launch of a UCO collection programme.

“It marks the beginning of a new circular economy for Vietnam; one where everyday waste becomes a valuable resource that contributes to cleaner skies and a more sustainable future. By combining FatHopes Energy’s expertise in digital traceability, feedstock collection and SAF supply chains with PVOIL’s nationwide reach and operational capabilities, we are building the infrastructure needed to support Vietnam’s energy transition while strengthening Southeast Asia’s role in the global sustainable aviation ecosystem.”

title: Canadian farm worker numbers take significant nosedive - Grainews
description:
Glacier FarmMedia — The number of people employed in Canadian agriculture has plummeted since 2020, dropping by about 52,000 workers.
In June 2020, 277,700 people reported working in agricultural jobs, says data from the Labour Force Survey, a Statistics Canada program.
The Labour Force Survey is a household poll, done monthly by StatCan.
Is it possible the Labour Force Survey from Statistics Canada may not capture the population of foreign workers who have jobs in Canadian agriculture?

text:
Glacier FarmMedia — The number of people employed in Canadian agriculture has plummeted since 2020, dropping by about 52,000 workers.

In June 2020, 277,700 people reported working in agricultural jobs, says data from the Labour Force Survey, a Statistics Canada program.

In June 2026, about 225,000 people said they were employed in agriculture. That’s a decline of 19 per cent in six years.

The Labour Force Survey is a household poll, done monthly by StatCan. The data provides information on labour market trends and “shifts in employment” within industrial sectors, says the StatCan website.

Julain Alvarez, a Statistics Canada analyst, said the survey results are reliable.

“Absolutely. We conduct the survey (for) about 65,000 households every month,” he said.

“We random sample … and for a span of six months people respond to the survey…. Our response rate is about 80 per cent.… We are very confident about the data.”

The Labour Force Survey classifies people who work in agriculture into the following sub-categories:

Crop production.

Animal production and aquaculture.

Support activities for crop production or animal production.

Farming not classified elsewhere, which could be areas such as maple syrup harvesting or seed production.

Sometimes, agriculture is lumped together with other industries for statistical collection, but this data and the job numbers are directly connnected to crops, livestock and farming employment, said a Statistics Canada spokesperson.

“Forestry, logging, fishing and hunting are not included in the agriculture industry. Instead, these activities are classified within a separate LFS (Labour Force Survey) industry grouping.”

Worker numbers have declined for decades

Historical data shows the number of people working in Canadian agriculture has dropped, consistently, over the last 50 to 60 years.

“I look at numbers from September of 1993. There were 400,000 people employed in agriculture,” Alvarez said.

“Almost twice the amount we see today.”

A line graph from Statistics Canada illustrates his point. About 350,000 people reported having agricultural jobs in 2006 and 220,000 in 2026.

However, the decline has accelerated since 2020, with a severe plunge on the graph and the number of workers.

Some of that is connected to COVID-19 and restrictions that forced Canadians to stay home.

From April 2021 to April 2022, about 21,000 fewer people were employed in agriculture

However, following the peak of the pandemic, the number of people employed in agriculture continued to slide. It went from 256,000 in June 2023 to 237,000 in June 2025.

The sinking numbers are connected to the labour shortfall in the industry, says the Canadian Agricultural Human Resource Council.

Farmers and agricultural businesses say it’s nearly impossible to find employees for available positions.

“More than 28,200 jobs were estimated to have gone unfilled in the agriculture sector during the peak season in 2022,” said a CAHRC report from 2024.

The Statistics Canada labour force data, showing a 52,000 person decline in the number of people employed in farming since 2020, can be explained by the chronic labour shortage in agriculture, said Jennifer Wright, CAHRC executive director.

“(This is) driven by an aging workforce, retirements, insufficient numbers of young people entering the sector, competition for talent from other industries,” she said.

“Lower levels of employment do not necessarily mean that labour demand has declined. It simply indicates that employers were unable to recruit the workers they needed.”

Missing temporary foreign workers?

Certain sectors within Canadian agriculture, including beekeepers, pork producers, feedlots and vegetable growers, rely heavily on temporary foreign workers, who come to Canada for the growing season or live in the country year-round.

Is it possible the Labour Force Survey from Statistics Canada may not capture the population of foreign workers who have jobs in Canadian agriculture?

The survey is thorough and considers all people, including Canadian citizens, permanent residents and non-permanent residents, Alvarez said.

“(It) is randomized and it works geographically…. They (get) addresses and if there’s a NPR (non-permanent resident) living at that address, then (they respond).”

Still, is it realistic to get non-permanent residents to respond to a government survey? Maybe the job numbers for agriculture are missing temporary foreign workers.

A Statistics Canada spokesperson said the agency takes precautions to ensure that the responses and data are representative of Canadians, permanent residents and non-permanent residents.

“As a standard statistical practice, responses provided by LFS (Labour Force Survey) respondents are weighted so that the sample of respondents is representative of the total population,” she said.

“The population totals used in this weighting process include non-permanent residents.”

Having 52,000 fewer people working in agricultural jobs, compared to six years ago, is not a statistical error. It could mean that the labour crisis in agriculture is even worse than reported. Anecdotal evidence and job postings indicate that grain, livestock and horticultural producers are desperate for employees.

The saskjobs.ca website, as of Aug. 11, had 172 help wanted postings for farm jobs in Saskatchewan. The available positions include combine operator, dairy herdsperson, apiary workers, general farm worker and farm truck driver, to name a few. That is just one employment website for Saskatchewan, and it doesn’t include the farmers who have given up on finding employees.

“CAHRC estimates that tens of thousands of agricultural positions remain unfilled during peak seasons,” Wright said.

text:
Driving reliability, efficiency and lifecycle value in next‑generation SAF plants

KROHNE 11 Aug, 2026: a leading provider of industrial process instrumentation, highlights its process instrumentation portfolio engineered for the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market. The portfolio enables producers to manage challenging feedstocks, hydrogen service, and demanding process conditions ranging from pretreatment through the final downstream process. As SAF projects move from first-of-a-kind plants toward larger-scale deployment, engineers are under pressure to upscale the process while maintaining reliable, economically viable production assets.

The SAF value chain brings together two distinct domains: conventional oil and gas refining and the production of renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil, edible oils, ethanol and biogas. This combination introduces process complexity across the entire process chain, including feedstock pretreatment, hydrotreatment and isomerization, hydrogen management and custody transfer. Each stage requires robust, application-specific measurement solutions to ensure safe, reliable and efficient operation.

“The SAF industry brings together two very different worlds,” says Yannick Farine, Industry Manager Biofuels and Bioenergy at KROHNE. “Success depends on understanding the behavior of renewable feedstocks upstream while also meeting the demands of downstream refining. Our goal is to help customers optimize processes, reduce maintenance and build SAF plants they can rely on for years to come”.

KROHNE offers a full range of standard instrumentation for flow & level, complemented by specialized devices for the most demanding SAF applications. Building on its installed base in edible oils, ethanol, biogas, and its extensive experience in oil & gas, the company is combining its experiencesthat aligns instrument selection with the specific challenges of the SAF process at every stage.

A central element of this concept is the wider use of ultrasonic flowmeters in SAF service. Unlike many traditional technologies, ultrasonic flowmeters have no internal restrictions, capillaries or moving parts and are well suited to abrasive feedstocks, hydrogen-rich streams, high-pressure steam and other critical services. And as the cherry on top, remain affordable. Their ability to operate at temperatures up to 600C and at high pressures for both liquids and gases makes them one of the few technologies capable of delivering accurate measurement across a broad envelope of SAF conditions. Advanced noise-filtering in ultrasonic gas flowmeters also supports reliable hydrogen measurement, which can be challenging due to the gas’s high velocity of sound and demanding operating environment.

Where maximum accuracy and direct mass measurement are required, KROHNE emphasizes single straight tube Coriolis mass flowmeters for abrasive feedstock and two-phase flow applications. Classic bent-tube designs can be susceptible to wear & tear, and risk performance issues under these conditions. Whereas straight tube configurations boast a full-bore design, which results in significantly less wear and so extend service life. Entrained gas management technology allows these meters to operate reliably under two-phase conditions at temperatures up to 400C, helping operators to maintain mass balance and yield monitoring even under challenging flow regimes. These capabilities are directly aligned with the mass-balance and yield-optimisation priorities identified for renewable diesel and SAF units in the attached measurement guidance.

KROHNE’s SAF approach also addresses the cost side of plant operation. Feedstock variability, hydrogen utilization and maintenance needs are identified as major cost drivers in the SAF production chain, and the company’s strategy is to use robust, well-matched instrumentation to reduce unplanned interventions, extend equipment life and lower overall operating expenditure. Alongside individual devices, KROHNE supplies tailored, integrated solutions intended to match the specific requirements of SAF plants, from Custody Transfer metering skids to leak detection systems to blending skids and much more.

By combining experience in conventional refining with application knowledge in renewable feedstocks, KROHNE aims to support SAF project developers, EPCs and operators with unique measurement solutions that contribute directly to process stability, safety and lifecycle economics.

title: How e-SAF Is Transforming the Future of Aviation Fuel - LG Chem Blog
description:
